articles.title: Trump administration to revoke visas of short-term visitors seeking asylum
articles.summary: The state department says the number of revocations "remains dynamic" and would be carried out on a rolling basis.
articles.body:
The Trump administration plans to revoke the visas of foreign nationals who entered the US as short-term visitors and later applied for asylum.

"Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud - which is grounds for visa revocation," US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said.

Pigott said the number of revocations "remains dynamic" and would be carried out on a rolling basis. US media reports suggest hundreds of thousands of visas could be affected.

Since President Donald Trump took office, his administration has revoked more than 175,000 visas held by foreign nationals on various grounds, according to the State Department.

"Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio's leadership, we are making clear that a visa is a privilege — not a right," Pigott said in a statement to the BBC.

He said that the department is coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security to identify and revoke nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then filed for asylum to stay permanently.

"These types of visas are issued with the clear understanding that they are for those who intend to return home," he said.

Those who apply for those so-called short-term B1 and B2 visas are asked to pledge that they will not apply for asylum in the US.

Holders of B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026, who have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, will be revoked, the Associated Press reported, citing State Department documents.

The majority of business and tourism visas in 2024 were issued to citizens from Brazil, which obtained more than 1.1m B1 and B2 visas, mainland China, India and Pakistan, according to State Department data.

Just over 32,300 were issued to visitors from Great Britain and Northern Ireland in 2024.

Earlier this month, the state department said it had revoked more than 175,000 visas from foreign nationals who it said "violated the terms of their visas, committed crimes, called for violence against US citizens, defrauded Americans, abused our immigration system, or endangered national security".

The state department recently told embassies and consulates to reschedule visa interviews so that consular officers can complete training on a more restrictive policy.

The visa revocations come after a US judge last week struck down Trump's visa ban covering 75 countries, ruling that the policy - introduced when Trump returned to office in January 2025 - exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio's statutory authority.

In June, another US judge ruled against the administration's efforts to halt the processing of immigration applications from 39 countries.

articles.title: Syria ‘shakes off’ past with removal from US ‘terror’ list, says al-Sharaa
articles.summary: Removal of decades-old designation offers major sanctions relief for Syria, aiming to boost post-war reconstruction.
articles.body:
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa hailed the United States’ removal of his country from the “state sponsors of terrorism” list, a major sanctions relief step for a country aiming to boost post-war reconstruction.

“Today, Syria shakes off a dark stain and tears away a painful chapter of its past to embark on a path of development, reconstruction and rebuilding,” al-Sharaa said in a speech.

list 2 of 4 Syria, Israel hold US-mediated talks in Jordan to de-escalate tensions

list 3 of 4 ‘Barrel bomb mufti’ sentenced to life in Syria

list 4 of 4 US removes Syria from ‘state sponsor of terrorism’ list

Washington’s decision on Monday rescinded a decades-old designation that came with severe economic restrictions, marking another step in warming ties between the countries following the 2024 ouster of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad.

Al-Sharaa expressed his “many thanks to the President of the United States of America, Donald Trump, and to all the friendly and supportive nations that stood by us”.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement that Monday’s move “will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability”.

But the Treasury stressed that its removal of restrictions on Syria “does not change Treasury’s posture with regards to countering global terrorism and our commitment to hold bad actors in Syria accountable”.

The US listed Syria as a “state sponsor of terrorism” in 1979, accusing the country, then under the rule of Hafez al-Assad, Bashar’s father, of supporting Palestinian fighter groups and other armed movements in neighbouring Lebanon.

Monday’s move gave Syria “a path to prosperity”, according to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The action “eliminates the final major barriers for private sector investment in Syria and promotes Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy,” he said in a statement.

The World Bank estimates post-war reconstruction to cost more than $216bn.

Several countries welcomed the US move. Turkiye, a key backer of Syria’s new authorities, said the decision will “lend momentum to efforts to strengthen Syria’s ties with the international community and to establish lasting security and stability in the country”.

“At this stage, we call on the international community to unite its efforts toward the goal of a prosperous Syria and to fulfill its responsibilities to bring an end to aggressive actions that jeopardize this vision,” Ankara said.

Qatar and Jordan also welcomed the US decision, saying the move would support stability and recovery efforts in the country.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement that the step “supports the path of a political settlement in line with international legitimacy resolutions and the aspirations of the Syrian people”.

Jordan’s Foreign Ministry also welcomed the US decision, calling it “an important step” towards supporting Syria’s reconstruction, recovery and development.

Welcoming the move, Saudi Arabia wished Syria “further security, stability, and prosperity, and continued progress in its reconstruction and development efforts” in a way that would benefit the “aspirations of its people”.

Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X that Ukraine had consistently supported Syria’s new government and people since the ouster of the Assad regime in their efforts to achieve recovery, peace and development.

In another sign of Syria’s growing international reintegration, Damascus also moved to expand its diplomatic outreach on Monday by launching an English-language social media account for its foreign media department.

Syrian Airlines will also begin operating regular direct flights from Damascus to Denmark’s capital, Copenhagen, and Austria’s capital, Vienna, on September 21, Syria’s civil aviation authority announced.

Omar al-Hosary, head of Syria’s General Authority of Civil Aviation and Air Transport, told the SANA news agency that the new routes are part of continuing efforts to expand the national carrier’s international network and strengthen air links between Syria and Europe.

articles.title: Dolly Parton obituary: The country legend who sang from the heart
articles.summary: The singer, songwriter and actress is known for timeless hits including Jolene and I Will Always Love You.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, the country singer from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, will be remembered for her songs that told beautiful stories so honestly, such as Coat of Many Colors, Jolene and I Will Always Love You.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.

Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy.”

She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her showbusiness career that spanned more than 60 years.

Dolly Rebecca Parton was born in 1946, the fourth of 12 children, into a poor farming family who lived in a one-bedroom cabin in Tennessee.

Her father, Robert Lee Parton, was a tobacco farmer and paid a missionary a sack of cornmeal for delivering her.

There was already music in the family - her mother, Avie Lee, sang folk songs all the time and her aunt played the guitar and wrote songs.

During some of Parton's earliest performances, her uncle, Bill Owens, accompanied her on the guitar - formative years for the future music legend.

From the age of six, she sang in the local church where her grandfather was the pastor, and was performing on her local TV station by the time she was a teenager.

In 1959, when she was 13 years old, Parton performed with Uncle Bill at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville - a live broadcast that is regarded as country music's biggest stage.

She was introduced by Johnny Cash and received three encores.

During her teenage years, Parton began to model herself on a local character who was known as the “town tramp”.

The lady wore bright red nail polish, low-cut tops and high heels - young Dolly thought she was beautiful.

When people said to her: “She ain’t nothing but trash”, Parton would reply: "Well, that’s what I’m gonna be when I grow up”.

Parton sang “ I’m just a backwards Barbie / too much make-up, too much hair ”, but her image was both a coat of armour and an astute disguise that helped get her noticed in showbusiness.

She would get ahead of the jokes by making them first, and had a quick and simple response for anyone who suggested she should tone it down: "Go to hell."

After graduating from high school in 1964, she moved to Nashville to launch her singing career and met her future husband, Carl Dean, on her very first day.

They married two years later and remained together until his death in 2025.

In Nashville, Parton's singing caught the eye of country performer Porter Wagoner, who hired her to perform on his television programme.

Over the next seven years, the pair became one of country music's most popular duos, releasing so many duets that many fans assumed they were a couple.

But their relationship was a complicated one, and as Parton's solo career started to rise, so did tensions behind the scenes.

Writing in her book Star of the Show: My Life on Stage, Parton said Wagoner saw her success away from his show as a "threat".

While travelling with Wagoner on a tour bus in 1969, Parton wrote Coat of Many Colors, a beautifully emotive tale of how she grew up poor, but rich with love.

Scrawled on the back of one of Wagoner's dry cleaning receipts, it was rated by Rolling Stone magazine as her second best-ever song. Years later, Parton named her own children's book Coat of Many Colors, and it was the name of a 2015 TV movie based on her life.

"It's a song that's just stood by me... it's created a life of many colours for me," she said.

Despite being unable to read sheet music, Parton played several instruments including the banjo, harp, piano and saxophone.

She had her first number one hit - and first Grammy nomination - with the song Joshua in 1971 and finally left The Porter Wagoner Show in 1974 to concentrate on her solo career.

To say goodbye to him, she wrote I Will Always Love You , a song that many think is about two lovers parting ways.

"That's the prettiest song I ever heard," Wagoner cried when he first heard it, her website says.

The same year, Elvis Presley was set to record a cover of the song, but Parton pulled the deal when his manager demanded half of the songwriting rights.

She cried all night at the difficult decision, and Priscilla Presley later told her that Elvis sang the song to her during their divorce.

In 1992, Whitney Houston transformed it into a now-iconic power ballad.

Parton said she was driving when she first heard the cover and had to pull over: “When I heard her go from the a cappella into the music part, I honestly thought I was going to have a heart attack, it was one of the most overwhelming things.”

Houston's cover of Parton's “sad little country song” was one of the proudest moments of her life, she said.

Parton re-recorded the song for The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, a 1982 film in which she starred and was nominated for a Golden Globe for best actress.

Another of her most famous songs was released in 1974 - Jolene.

Showing her aching vulnerability, it's about a bank clerk with flaming locks of auburn hair who flirted with her husband.

" Jolene, I'm begging of you, please don't take my man ," she pleads.

Parton said her husband, who was notoriously private, was a bit embarrassed by the song. But it was nothing serious - just a running joke between them: "I was saying, 'Hell, you're spending a lot of time at the bank. I don't believe we've got that kind of money.'"

The song has been covered by many artists including The White Stripes, Miley Cyrus and Beyoncé, who changed up the lyrics to the more ominous: " I'm warning you, don't come for my man. "

In the years to come, Dolly Parton's success only grew, with more hits, nominations and awards - she won her first Grammy in 1978 for Here You Come Again.

It was the theme song that Dolly Parton wrote for the 1980 movie 9 to 5 that fully propelled her to stardom.

Actress Jane Fonda, who produced and starred in the film about women being discriminated against in the workplace, made a deal with Parton - she'd star in the film if she could also write the theme song.

Realising her nails clicking together sounded like a typewriter, she wrote 9 to 5 while waiting around on set. Fonda said she realised straight away that it wasn't just a theme song - it was an anthem.

The film was a big success at the box office and the song won several awards, including a Golden Globe.

'I look like a woman but I think like a man'

Parton was a successful and shrewd businesswoman, and in 2022 was listed by Forbes as one of America's richest self-made women .

"I look like a woman but I think like a man. I've done business with men who think I'm as silly as I look. By the time they realise I'm not, I've got the money and gone," she once said.

Her physical appearance - the costumes, wigs, long painted nails and high heels - were merely a facade of a stereotypical “dumb blonde”. But she always said she knew she wasn't dumb "and I also know that I'm not blonde".

She had her own record label, Dolly Records, and co-owned The Dollywood Company, which manages entertainment venues, a theme park, a water park and a resort.

In 1986, she opened her Dollywood amusement park in the foothills of her beloved Smoky Mountains. As well as rollercoasters, it is home to the largest sanctuary for non-releasable bald eagles in the world. Its rehabilitation and breeding work has won awards and in 2007, the bald eagle was removed from the endangered species list.

Despite her wealth and success, Parton remained humble and supported the communities where she grew up.

Inspired by her father who couldn’t read or write, she launched the Imagination Library in 1999, which gave free books to children in Tennessee. It has since expanded to Australia, the UK, Ireland and Canada, sending out millions of free books every year.

Her non-profit organisation, The Dollywood Foundation, has funded scholarships, hospitals and donated to flood and wildfire victims.

In 2020, as the Covid-19 pandemic gripped the world, Parton donated $1m (£716,000) to the Vanderbilt University Medical Centre which helped to fund the Moderna vaccine.

How Dolly Parton became the world’s best-loved celebrity

In later years, Parton had to postpone or cancel several shows for health treatment.

In May 2026, she postponed an upcoming Las Vegas residency because of treatment for kidney stones, saying it would take some time to heal and be "stage-performance ready".

"I can't be dizzy carrying around banjos, guitars and such on five-inch heels - and you know that I'm going to be wearing them," she said in a video message.

"Not to mention all those heavy rhinestone outfits, the big hair, my big... uh, personality," she joked.

Parton spoke graciously throughout her career with humour and intelligence. She steered clear of politics, saying she didn't want to alienate half her audience.

She was a courageous and talented trailblazer for country music at a time when women were not taken seriously in the industry, especially as solo artists.

Parton said she hoped to be remembered for her songwriting and as somebody who took her work seriously, but not herself.

She once offered this advice: “Never ignore your roots, your home, or your hair."

It's guidance that she stayed true to throughout her life.

articles.title: Georgia sheriff seizes 1,800 pounds of suspected black-market marijuana shipped from California
articles.summary: A 1,800-pound black market marijuana shipment from Sacramento, California, was intercepted in Georgia, reportedly bound for Atlanta and Orlando.
articles.body: A massive shipment of 1,800 pounds of suspected black-market marijuana from California was intercepted in Georgia on Tuesday, with authorities saying the drugs were destined for Atlanta and Orlando. The shipment originated in Sacramento, where recreational marijuana is legal, according to the Butts County Sheriff’s Office. Sheriff Gary Long said about half of the marijuana was bound for Atlanta, while the rest was headed to Orlando. The sheriff’s office did not say where or how the shipment was intercepted, whether anyone was arrested or whether charges were filed. NY TIMES WALKS BACK STANCE ON MARIJUANA LEGALIZATION, ADMITS LOOSENING OF POLICIES HAS MADE COUNTRY WORSE OFF Long used the seizure to make his case that legalizing marijuana does not eliminate illegal sales. "But here is the reality: the black market isn't going away," Long said in a press release announcing the seizure. Marijuana laws vary among the three states connected to the shipment. California allows recreational marijuana, while Georgia and Florida allow marijuana only for certain medical uses. "The illegal marijuana trade does not stop at the state line," Long said. Long said Mexican drug-trafficking organizations and other criminal groups continue to move large amounts of marijuana across state lines. The sheriff’s office did not say the shipment seized Tuesday was connected to a cartel or any other criminal organization. The sheriff also argued that illegal sellers can undercut licensed marijuana businesses because they don't pay taxes or licensing fees or have to follow testing and other regulatory requirements. "As long as there is demand and money to be made, illegal dealers will continue to operate," Long said. AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING Long urged Georgia lawmakers to look closely at what has happened in states that have legalized marijuana before making changes to Georgia's laws. He pointed to California, which has changed its cannabis tax and regulatory system while continuing to fight illegal marijuana sales. He also cited past ballot initiatives filed in Colorado seeking to repeal constitutional provisions that legalized recreational marijuana, though those efforts did not reverse legalization. "That should be a warning to Georgia," Long said. "We should learn from the experiences of states that have already gone down this road instead of repeating the same mistakes and then spending years trying to fix them." Long said his statement was not meant to settle the question of whether marijuana should be legal. Instead, he argued that lawmakers need to consider how illegal sales and trafficking would fit into any changes to Georgia law. articles.title: Pakistan, Iran made ‘significant progress’ to end US-Iran war, minister says
articles.summary: Pakistan and Iran on Tuesday announced that “significant progress” has been made toward ending the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, according to Pakistan’s interior minister, Reuters reported. Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, met with Iranian officials in Tehran about measures to prevent the conflict from growing and to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which…
articles.body:
Pakistan and Iran on Tuesday announced that “significant progress” has been made toward ending the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, according to Pakistan’s interior minister, Reuters reported .

Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, met with Iranian officials in Tehran about measures to prevent the conflict from growing and to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed under Iranian control, causing gas prices to skyrocket.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who traveled with Munir, said their meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was “very positive and productive.”

“The Iranian President candidly shared his Government’s perspective and concerns, and we had a very constructive exchange on the issues involved,” Naqvi wrote on the social platform X . “Significant progress was made, and the meeting concluded on a highly positive note. We remain hopeful that this momentum will help pave the way for further progress and lasting peace in the region.”

Naqvi said the discussion focused on the conflict and a path forward for the region. He added that they talked about the steps needed to restore the interim peace deal signed by the U.S. and Iran in June, which expired last week.

Munir called President Trump ahead of the talks in Tehran, Reuters reported.

The Pakistani delegation’s visit comes as Iran and Oman announced a plan to allow navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and clear mines placed in the waterway. Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi met with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Tehran about a “phased framework” for the strait.

“The proposed framework includes the establishment of a joint temporary navigational corridor through the Strait of Hormuz and an agreement to implement a joint project to clear the Strait of mines,” Oman’s Foreign Ministry posted on the social platform X .

Talks regarding the strait’s future would include an agreement on “a mechanism for information-sharing, traffic management, and the provision of relevant navigational and security services.”

“In this context, both sides underscored the importance of convening joint discussions with regional states bordering the waters of the Gulf,” the foreign minister’s office added. “They further stressed the need to uphold applicable international law and respect the sovereign rights of the coastal states.”

Trump previously threatened Oman over potentially striking a deal with Iran, warning the country that “we’ll bomb the s— out of them” if it “gets in the way.”

Iranian officials have insisted that the strait will reopen after Trump withdraws a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, pays compensation for damages from the war, lifts sanctions and unfreezes assets.

The Trump administration has also warned other countries that they could face economic consequences if they do not cut off their financial ties to the Iranian regime. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced “ Operation Economic Outcast ,” a new campaign to constrict Iran’s economy, but offered few specific details.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior, why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent said in response to a reporter’s question about the operation’s details.

articles.title: Archaeologists found two young horses buried beside a Bronze Age tomb in Germany; the 3,000-year-old ritual may reveal an ancient sacrifice
articles.summary: Europe News: Archaeologists excavating near Nauendorf in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, have uncovered the remains of two very young horses deliberately buried beside a L.
articles.body: Archaeologists excavating near Nauendorf in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, have uncovered the remains of two very young horses deliberately buried beside a Late Bronze Age burial mound, offering rare evidence of ritual animal sacrifice more than 3,000 years ago. The discovery was made during archaeological investigations ahead of construction of the SuedOstLink electricity transmission line, which exposed a prehistoric landscape containing settlements, graves and other features. At the centre of the find were the remains of a burial mound dating to the beginning of the Late Bronze Age, although the mound itself had long since disappeared beneath the flat landscape. Archaeologists identified its former outline from a circular ditch and found two stone-lined human graves inside the enclosure itself. They then unexpectedly discovered a horse buried in the ditch, followed 11 metres northeast by a second horse placed in the same orientation as the human graves. Both animals were foals only about five to nine months old when they were deliberately deposited.How archaeologists uncovered a forgotten Bronze Age burial moundThe excavation took place at Nauendorf in the northern Saalekreis district as part of archaeological investigations preceding construction of the SuedOstLink electricity transmission route. The wider site contains evidence of a settlement landscape dating from the Late Bronze Age and Iron Age, including house locations, storage pits, oven pits, ditches and a burial ground. Among the earliest features was a burial mound dating to the beginning of the Late Bronze Age.The mound itself was no longer visible as a raised feature because centuries of erosion and agricultural activity had flattened the landscape. Archaeologists could nevertheless identify its former location from the circular ditch surrounding it, with an earthen bridge or entrance surviving on the eastern side. Inside the enclosure were 2 elongated, stone-lined graves. The excavation therefore revealed not simply isolated horse remains, but an unusual concentration of animal and human funerary features within the same archaeological monument.Why the discovery of 2 horses inside the burial monument was unexpectedArchaeologists initially encountered the remains of a horse in a deeper pit cut into the southeastern section of the circular ditch. Such pits can contain later human burials, but in this case the excavation revealed a horse lying on its right side instead. When the excavation area was expanded, researchers discovered a second horse only 11 metres northeast of the first.The second animal had also been deliberately placed on its side and was oriented identically to the 2 stone-lined graves inside the burial mound. The State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt describes this alignment as an obvious reference to the graves, providing strong evidence that the horse burial was deliberately connected to the funerary monument rather than being an unrelated animal deposit.Why the 2 animals were probably deliberately sacrificedBoth horses were exceptionally young foals, approximately 5 to 9 months old. Although their skeletons were only partially preserved, particularly because of their young age, the surviving skulls and long bones show that the animals were originally deposited as complete carcasses rather than as selected body parts. Both were lying on their right sides with their limbs naturally bent.One foal has another unusual feature. Its hind-leg bones lie almost parallel to each other, which archaeologists interpret as a possible indication that its body had been bound or constricted around the hindquarters before burial. This remains an interpretation rather than proof of exactly how the animal was handled or killed.Radiocarbon dating places the 2 deposits in essentially the same period. The first foal produced a calibrated date of 1212â1055 BCE, while the second dates to 1211â1052 BCE, both within the beginning of the Late Bronze Age. The State Office describes the discovery as a previously singular example of the ritual deposition of such young horses during this period.Why sacrificing 2 young horses would have been significantHorses had a status in Bronze Age societies that extended well beyond their value as ordinary livestock. The State Office notes that their importance increasingly shifted during the Bronze Age from that of a food animal toward that of a prestige object associated with wealth, mobility, religious beliefs and burial practices. Evidence for this changing status appears in rock art, decorated pottery, bronze objects and elaborate horse harnesses deposited in graves and hoards.That makes the age of the Nauendorf animals particularly significant. A foal only a few months old represented an animal with years of potential economic value ahead of it. Deliberately sacrificing and removing 2 such animals from future use would therefore have represented a meaningful expenditure of resources. The archaeological interpretation is that their sacrifice may reflect the importance of the funerary ritual and potentially the elevated status of the people buried beneath the mound. The exact religious meaning, however, cannot be established from the surviving evidence. The archaeologists can identify the deliberate deposition, the animals' young age, their placement near the mound and their relationship to the human graves, but they cannot reconstruct precisely what the ceremony meant to the people who carried it out.How rare complete Bronze Age horse burials areSaxony-Anhalt already has numerous archaeological finds showing that horses or horse parts could form part of prehistoric funerary practices. The State Office specifically cites discoveries at Esperstedt, Burgsdorf and GroÃpasleben, among other sites.Those discoveries include individual horse bones, skulls and lower-leg bones, as well as combinations of selected skeletal parts. Complete horse burials from this period are considerably rarer. Comparable examples have been reported only sporadically in the neighbouring Lusatian cultural area, where horses associated with funerary practices appear to have been cremated and their remains placed in ceramic vessels. The Nauendorf discovery is therefore unusual not simply because horses were involved, but because 2 very young animals appear to have been deposited as complete carcasses in direct association with the same burial monument.What the 2 foals reveal about Bronze Age beliefsThe discovery provides a rare physical glimpse into how Bronze Age communities connected animals, status and death. The horses were not simply discarded remains: their deliberate placement within the area of the burial mound, their alignment and their young age all point toward a purposeful act.The strongest interpretation from the archaeological evidence is that the animals were sacrificed as part of a ritual connected with the burial monument. Their sacrifice may have expressed the status of the people buried there, accompanied the deceased symbolically or fulfilled another religious purpose that is now impossible to reconstruct.More than 3,000 years later, the 2 foals preserve evidence of that decision in the archaeological record. Their bones show that horses could occupy a place in Bronze Age funerary practice that went far beyond their practical economic value.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces group says it has dissolved after merging with the Syrian army
articles.summary: The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces on Tuesday announced the official dissolution of the group, which once controlled a de facto autono...
articles.body:
DAMASCUS, Syria (AP) — The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces on Tuesday announced the official dissolution of the group, which once controlled a de facto autonomous zone in Syria's northeast.

Speaking during a news conference at the presidential palace in Damascus, Mazloum Abdi said the SDF has completed a merger with the Syrian army and would cease to operate as an independent force. The Kurdish-led force lost most of its territory in northeast Syria to a government offensive in January and then signed the deal to merge with the army.

The SDF was once the main partner of the United States in Syria as it battled the Islamic State group. But after the ouster of former Syrian President Bashar Assad in December 2024, Washington formed close ties with the new government in Damascus led by interim Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa, the former leader of an Islamist insurgent group.

The SDF "carried a heavy responsibility during one of the most difficult periods in Syria's history," Abdi said.

"Today, circumstances have changed, and the country has entered a new phase, one of peace and participation in building a new Syria," he said, announcing the "end of the SDF's mission" and "its dissolution as an independent military force."

Under the 50-year rule of the Assad dynasty in Syria, Kurds were marginalized, with many denied citizenship. Public celebrations of the Nowruz holiday — an ancient Persian springtime new year festival that is also celebrated by Kurds in Syria, Turkey and Iraq as well as Iran — were banned.

Shortly after the uprising against the Assad government began in 2011, the Kurds filled the vacuum created by the withdrawal of government forces from wide areas of Syria's northeast. The SDF at one point controlled about 25% of Syria.

The Kurds were initially circumspect about the new post-Assad government and unwilling to give up their de facto autonomy. Some of the insurgent groups that took part in the offensive that ousted Assad were Turkish-backed forces that had clashed with the SDF in the past.

Turkey considered the SDF to be a terrorist organization because of its ties to the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK, a separatist group that staged a decades-long insurgency in Turkey. A peace process is now underway.

Kurds questioned whether the new Sunni Arab-led authorities would give them true representation in the new government, while al-Sharaa tried to woo them.

During ceasefire negotiations with the SDF in January, he issued a decree strengthening Kurdish rights. It made Kurdish an official language along with Arabic, and adopted Nowruz as a national holiday. It also restored the citizenship of tens of thousands of Kurds in northeastern Hassakeh province after they were stripped of it during the 1962 census.

Abdi said that al-Sharaa had promised that Kurds would have the right to education in their own language, an important issue for the country's Kurdish population.

Questions remain, including the fate of the SDF's all-female fighting units — a sensitive point in the integration talks as many of the Damascus leaders come from a conservative background and are opposed to women in combat.

But the success of the integration agreement with the SDF is a major boost to al-Sharaa's government, which has struggled to unify the country as it begins to recover from a nearly 14-year civil war. Most of the country is now under the control of the central government in Damascus.

The exception is southern Syria's Sweida province, which is now controlled by Druze factions that are hostile to Damascus after clashes last year in which government-affiliated fighters launched sectarian revenge attacks on Druze civilians. The Druze factions have received support from Israel, which is also occupying a strip of land in southern Syria near the border with the Israeli-annexed Golan Heights.

articles.title: New Mexico has protected nearly 11,000 acres along the Mimbres River as a new wildlife area, safeguarding historic water rights, rare river habitat and a 2-mile stretch of the desert stream
articles.summary: US News: Conservationists and state officials in New Mexico have completed a deal to buy nearly 11,000 acres of ecologically rich land along the Mimbres River,.
articles.body: Conservationists and state officials in New Mexico have completed a deal to buy nearly 11,000 acres of ecologically rich land along the Mimbres River, permanently protecting an important desert watershed and creating the state's newest public conservation preserve. The purchase secures the newly created Mimbres Ranch Wildlife Management Area (WMA), a large property bordering the Gila National Forest in southwestern New Mexico. The project was completed with help from the national non-profit Trust for Public Land (TPL) and the state government. The acquisition places about two miles of the Mimbres River under public ownership while protecting historic water rights that date back more than a century. The property also creates a large, connected area for native wildlife and expands public access along the scenic Trail of the Mountain Spirits Byway.Protecting water rights and desert habitatA key part of the deal is the permanent protection of important pre-1907 water rights connected to the Mimbres River. In the dry American Southwest, these water rights have major legal and environmental importance. They were established before New Mexico adopted its wider water code and have senior priority under state law. Protecting the rights will help keep water flowing through the river rather than being diverted for industrial or large-scale municipal use. This will support the river's surrounding riparian bosque, a green area of trees and plants that depends on the water. The Mimbres River is part of a rare closed-basin desert stream system. Its water stays within the basin instead of flowing into an ocean or another major river system. This unusual system has created a unique habitat for plants and animals adapted to the valley."At a time when public lands are under threat across the country, New Mexico is leaning in on conservation," said Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham in an official release published by the State of New Mexico Newsroom. "Protecting nearly 11,000 acres along the Mimbres River means healthier wildlife, cleaner water, and more places for New Mexico families to hunt, fish, and get outside. New Mexicans will benefit from this investment for generations to come."Protecting rare fish and wildlifeThe new wildlife management area contains a mix of Southwestern habitats, including high-desert grasslands, pinyon-juniper woodlands, cottonwood forests along the river and areas of ponderosa pine. These habitats support large animals such as Rocky Mountain elk, mule deer, black bears and mountain lions. They also provide habitat for birds including Merriam's turkey and quail. The property also contains designated critical habitat for federally protected species, including the western yellow-billed cuckoo and Chiricahua leopard frog. State fisheries biologists said the property is also important for protecting native fish found in the Mimbres drainage."This will create additional habitat for conserving the Rio Grande sucker and Chihuahua chub," said Kirk Patten, Chief of the Fisheries Management Division at the New Mexico Department of Game and Fish, in coverage reported by Organ Mountain News. "Both these fish are native to the Mimbres drainage, and this acquisition will ensure they continue to thrive there for years to come." The WMA will also connect with the Gila National Forest and existing protected areas, including The Nature Conservancy's Mimbres River Preserve. This will join previously separated habitats into a larger, more connected landscape.Broad support for the projectThe project received funding and legislative support through state conservation programmes, with environmental groups providing technical help. Representative Nathan Small, a Democrat from Las Cruces who supported funding for the project in the state legislature, highlighted the importance of the river and surrounding land. "Here in New Mexico, our land and water are sacred. The Mimbres River and its surrounding uplands vibrate with life, supporting hundreds of plant, animal, bird, and even rare fish species," Small stated in the official announcement published by Trust for Public Land. "The Mimbres Ranch WMA will enhance this ecosystem and create new recreation opportunities, including opportunities for New Mexico resident hunters." The property is also important for its history. It was once home to the ancient Mimbres culture, part of the Mogollon tradition and known for its distinctive black-on-white pottery made between about 1000 AD and 1150 AD.Jim Petterson, Mountain West Region Vice-President for the Trust for Public Land, said the purchase was the result of several years of cooperation between different groups. "This project represents a major win for wildlife, water and communities across New Mexico," said Petterson in an official press release. "By protecting this ecologically rich property, we are ensuring that this extraordinary landscape, home to rare species and critical waterways, will remain intact and accessible to the public for generations to come."State officials also described the acquisition as a long-term investment in conservation, tourism and outdoor recreation. "This acquisition represents an investment in the long-term sustainability of New Mexico's treasured wildlife, as well as its outdoor heritage," said Mike Sloane, Director of the New Mexico Department of Game and Fish, in statements carried by the Governor's Office. "Protecting this landscape helps conserve habitat for big game, native fish and other species, while creating new opportunities for the public to enjoy our state's outdoor spaces."Located near both the Gila Wilderness and the Aldo Leopold Wilderness, the Mimbres Ranch Wildlife Management Area is expected to eventually offer hiking, licensed seasonal hunting, horseback riding and bird watching. The New Mexico Department of Game and Fish said detailed management plans and rules for public access will be released after initial assessments of the property are completed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Immigrant dad of USS Lincoln sailor is released from ICE detention
articles.summary: Joshua Aviles posted a family statement on Facebook saying his father, Luis Manuel Aviles, “has been released back to our family.”
articles.body: The immigrant father of a sailor who is on board the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln is back with his family Tuesday after being detained by immigration authorities over the weekend. The family confirmed the release of Luis Manuel Aviles in a statement posted on social media by his son Joshua Aviles, a Navy handling airman. Joshua Aviles has been deployed on the aircraft carrier for nine months, which is considered a U.S. military record for uninterrupted time at sea. “Luis has been released back to our family. We are grateful for all of the support for both Luis and Josh throughout this situation. At this moment, our family is taking time to be together. While we await the return of our proud Navy sailor, we kindly ask for your understanding and respect,” the statement reads. The Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not respond to multiple requests for comment about the release of Luis Manuel Aviles. DHS confirmed over the weekend that Border Patrol arrested Luis Manuel Aviles on Saturday during a traffic stop in Key West, Florida, where the family lives. The agency said he entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown date and location and was being held in ICE custody. Originally from Nicaragua, Luis Manuel Aviles, 47, has been living in the U.S. for 20 years. He’s mostly worked as a handyman for hotels in Key West, according to his youngest son, Luis Aviles, and stepdaughter, Katty Delgado. In an interview with Noticias Telemundo on Sunday, Luis Aviles said his father “never hid, he always did things the right way,” adding that he was working toward getting legal status and had complied with his paperwork and visits to ICE’s offices. Delgado told NBC News on Saturday that her stepfather had a work permit, a Social Security card, a driver’s license and an active asylum case. Joshua Aviles, along with another family member, had filed immigration petitions requesting he remain in the country legally, according to the family. Asked to confirm whether Luis Manuel Aviles had a Social Security number, a work permit or pending immigration cases, as his family indicated, DHS said in an email Sunday, “Having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws.” “Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement,” the email reads. On the same weekend in which Luis Manuel Aviles was detained, the Key West Immigrant Support Network had been alerting immigrant communities in the area of an uptick in “immigration activity” following the detentions of three people Thursday afternoon. “We saw this surge of officers we didn’t recognize. We saw cars that we didn’t recognize,” said Heather Slivko-Bathurst, the director of the nonprofit immigrant rights organization. “All of a sudden, boom! It was 28 people detained in 72 hours.” After months of quiet immigration detentions, Slivko-Bathurst told NBC News, immigrant communities in Key West “saw this resurgence of almost like an operative type.” DHS and Customs and Border Protection did not respond to questions about their enforcement operations in Key West in recent weeks. They said in an email that “ICE agents uphold our nation’s immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day,” and cited the cases of several convicted criminals who were arrested in Florida. Slivko-Bathurst said the presence of Border Patrol in the area seemed particularly heightened Saturday morning, prompting the Key West Immigrant Support Network to share a post on Facebook at 9 a.m. saying, “If there is ever a day to be as careful as possible, it is today.” Later that morning, Luis Manuel Aviles was arrested by Border Patrol while running errands. He was among at least seven people immigration authorities detained in Key West on Saturday, according to Slivko-Bathurst. Her organization verified the immigration detentions of 28 people this week, and it has been in contact with the families of most of them, she said. Most of the detainees “have work authorizations and have been following the legal process to be in this country,” according to the group. The organization has also decried how its small Florida town has become “targeted on a huge level compared to our population size.” It’s estimated that nearly a quarter of the roughly 25,000 people who live in Key West are foreign-born residents, many of whom work in the hospitality and tourism industries, as well as in landscaping, construction and contract work, Slivko-Bathurst said. “Essentially, it boils down to the fact that we have a very large immigrant population, documented and undocumented,” Slivko-Bathurst added. “There is just this constant fear among everybody, because there’s not a single person in Key West — it’s a two-by-four island — that doesn’t know somebody who is an immigrant, whatever status they may have.” The detention of Luis Manuel Aviles gained national attention after his son, Joshua Aviles, posted about it Saturday on Facebook while on board the USS Abraham Lincoln. “I just got a call that my dad was taken by ICE. If you know my dad, you know he is a hardworking, humble man who is always willing to help anyone if he can,” the post reads. “We have done everything through immigration to get his green card approved, and we are just waiting.” The post continues: “This is heartbreaking for me. I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal. My dad’s only ‘crime’ was coming to this country to give my siblings and me a better life.” The Navy said Saturday that the Lincoln had officially left the Middle East en route to the West Coast, a journey that could take a month or more.

articles.title: In 1973, Dr Martin Cooper made world's first mobile phone call to his rival at Bell Labs; but all he heard back was silence as ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: âOn April 3, 1973, Motorola engineer Dr Martin Cooper made what is widely recognised as the first mobile phone call. Standing on a New York City stree.
articles.body: âOn April 3, 1973, Motorola engineer Dr Martin Cooper made what is widely recognised as the first mobile phone call. Standing on a New York City street, Cooper called Joel Engel, an engineer at Bell Laboratories and his rival in the race to develop mobile communications. Cooper told Engel he was calling from a âpersonal, handheld portable cell phone,â but all he heard back was silence as he presumed his competitor had been left speechless.âThe call came as Motorola and Bell Laboratories were pursuing different approaches to mobile communications. Bell Labs was working on car-based phones, while Cooper and Motorola were developing a device a person could carry. By making the call in the middle of a street rather than from a vehicle, Cooper demonstrated the idea of a truly portable mobile phone.âThe history of the first mobile phone callâIn the 1970s, Bell Laboratories was developing mobile phones designed for use inside cars. Motorola was pursuing a different approach that would allow people to carry their phones with them.âCooper's 1973 call was made using an early prototype that would eventually lead to the Motorola DynaTAC 8000X. The first mobile phone sold to consumers did not arrive until 1984, more than a decade after Cooper made his call.âThe DynaTAC 8000X was considerably different from the phones people use today. It could provide around 30 minutes of talk time, required about 10 hours to recharge and weighed roughly 1.7 pounds. Its price was also high, equivalent to about $11,700 in today's money.âThe 1973 demonstration was therefore not a consumer product launch. It showed that a mobile phone could operate independently of a vehicle and be carried by an individual.âWhy Martin Cooper called his Bell Labs rivalâCooper later explained that the call had a broader purpose beyond the competition between Motorola and Bell Labs. In a 2013 BGR interview marking the 40th anniversary of the call, he said his goal was to prevent AT&T, which owned Bell Laboratories at the time, from âcreating a monopoly in the cell phones. And not only that, but a monopoly in car telephones.ââCooper acknowledged that AT&T had invented cellular technology in 1947, but said Motorola did not want the company to become the sole provider once mobile phones reached consumers. âWe thought the world was ready for the freedom you get in having personal communications. And we sure didn't want to get put out of business.ââThe rivalry between the two companies was therefore connected to how mobile communications would develop and who would control the emerging market.âCooper later acknowledged that the call also had a competitive element. In 2023, he told NPR that he was ânot averse to rubbing [Engel's] nose in our achievement.ââThe exchange took place when mobile communications were still largely experimental. The phone Cooper used was bulky by modern standards and had limited battery life, but the call demonstrated that a person could make a wireless call without being connected to a vehicle.âMore than five decades later, mobile phones have evolved from large devices designed primarily for voice calls into computers used for messaging, photography, navigation, internet access and other functions. Cooper's 1973 call to Engel marked an early step in that transition.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Dolly Parton: A life in pictures
articles.summary: The singer rose from humble beginnings to become one of the most beloved entertainers in the world.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, the country music superstar from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, rose from humble beginnings to become one of the most beloved entertainers in the world.

Over a career spanning more than 60 years, she sold more than 100 million records, wrote more than 3,000 songs and won 11 Grammy Awards, including a lifetime achievement honour.

Yet she has always described herself first and foremost as a songwriter. "It's my way of expressing myself. It's my therapy," she once said.

Dolly Parton grew up in poverty in a one-room cabin on the banks of the Little Pigeon River in Tennessee's Smoky Mountains, the fourth of 12 children.

She performed on local radio and television as a child and recorded her first single at 13.

After moving to Nashville the day after graduating from Sevier County High School, Dolly Parton scored her first solo hit with Dumb Blonde in 1966.

In 1967, country star Porter Wagoner invited Parton to join The Porter Wagoner Show, giving her a regular role on his nationally syndicated television programme as well as a place in his touring stage show.

Her breakthrough came with the album Hello, I'm Dolly.

Dolly Parton became a member of the Grand Ole Opry on January 4, 1969.

She has described the Opry as the "church of my heart" and said performing there was a lifelong dream.

In one remarkable 1973 writing session, Parton penned two of her signature hits – Jolene and I Will Always Love You.

Having written thousands of songs across her decades-long career, Parton said songwriting was her greatest form of self-expression.

Known for her larger-than-life image, Dolly Parton combined rhinestones, wit and charm to sustain a career that crossed from country to mainstream pop.

She headlined festivals and became a global star with albums such as Here You Come Again.

Parton also became known for memorable collaborations, notably with Kenny Rogers, whose duet Islands in the Stream became one of the defining hits of the 1980s.

While Dolly Parton is best known for her decades-spanning music career, her work as an actor has also left a lasting impression on film audiences.

Parton's breakout screen role came in the 1980 workplace comedy 9 to 5, where she starred alongside Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin and Dabney Coleman.

Her portrayal of Doralee Rhodes combined comic timing with warmth, helping to redefine expectations of performers crossing over from music into film.

She followed this with roles in films such as The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, alongside Burt Reynolds, and Steel Magnolias.

The latter featured an ensemble cast including Julia Roberts and Sally Field alongside Sylvester Stallone.

In these performances, Parton demonstrated a balance of humour and emotional depth, often anchoring scenes with a distinctly understated presence.

In 1986 Dolly Parton opened Dollywood, a theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, near her birthplace.

It became a major tourist attraction - one of the most visited regional theme parks in the USA.

The park's success helped fund Parton's charitable foundation and literacy programme.

Through her Imagination Library, founded in honour of her father who could not read, Dolly Parton has given away more than 100 million free books to children around the world.

Her own book, Coat of Many Colours, was the 100 millionth book that programme donated to the US Library of Congress collection.

A council in Scotland announced it would dedicate a day to Dolly Parton every year to mark the impact of her reading scheme.

Parton personally donated millions to medical research and disaster relief.

The singer also led several major disaster-relief efforts, most notably creating the My People Fund after the 2016 Great Smoky Mountains wildfires which distributed about $10m to families who lost homes.

She lined up an all-star list of performers for a three-hour telethon to raise money.

In 2024, she pledged $2m for Hurricane Helene relief in East Tennessee and Appalachia, combining a personal donation with matching support from her businesses and foundation.

Parton's 2014 Glastonbury Festival appearance quickly became one of the defining "Legends" slot performances in the event's history.

Drawing one of the festival's biggest-ever daytime crowds - estimated at more than 180,000 - she turned the Pyramid Stage into a mass singalong, with renditions of Jolene, 9 to 5 and I Will Always Love You prompting scenes of near-universal audience participation.

In 2019, Parton celebrated 50 years as an Opry member with a major televised special called Dolly Parton: 50 Years at the Opry.

The event featured performances and tributes from other country artists.

Her decades-spanning relationship with the Opry helped cement its status as both a guardian of country music tradition and a stage for modern stars.

Parton gradually began to step away from major touring, saying she no longer wanted to spend long stretches on the road.

Instead, she focused on selective live shows, new recording projects and screen appearances including Dolly Parton's Heartstrings, Mountain Magic and Christmas on the Square for Netflix.

In 2021, Parton publicly received a Covid-19 vaccine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, using the moment to encourage others to do the same.

She sang an adapted version of her hit Jolene, singing: "Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, I'm begging of you, please don't hesitate."

Parton's 2022 induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame marked a characteristically self-aware turn.

Having initially said she had not "earned" the honour, she later embraced it with humour - declaring "I'm a rock star now" - before performing her new song Rockin', written especially for the ceremony, a symbolic step toward her later rock album Rockstar.

In 2023, Parton delivered another headline-grabbing live moment when she performed at the Dallas Cowboys' Thanksgiving halftime show, appearing in a rhinestone-studded Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders outfit.

More recently, Parton continued to balance personal loss with new creative work.

Following the death of her husband Carl Dean in 2025, she released If You Hadn't Been There in tribute, while also continuing development of Dolly: A True Original Musical, the stage production based on her life and career.

In early 2026, Parton gave a pre-recorded tribute speech for Ozzy Osbourne at the BRIT Awards in Manchester, where Ozzy received a posthumous Lifetime Achievement Award.

Her speech was short but was one of the emotional highlights of the ceremony.

Parton had been due to return to the stage for a short Las Vegas residency, but announced this month that she was cancelling the run because of health issues, telling fans she needed "a little more time to heal".

She will remain a cultural icon remembered for her generosity and humour, as well as her extraordinary songwriting - the craft at the heart of a catalogue that has shaped modern country music and crossed generations.

articles.title: Former TOPGUN pilot analyzes Marine Corps pilot's eerie calm after emergency F-18 ejection
articles.summary: Former TOPGUN pilot Matthew Buckley explains the violent forces of ejection and why Marine Corps Maj. Jackson Simon appeared so calm after his F-18 crash.
articles.body: Former TOPGUN pilot Matthew "Whiz" Buckley told Fox News Digital that the recent crash of a Marine Corps F-18 in Washington state — and the pilot's split-second decision to eject — highlights both the violence of the maneuver and how the ensuing shock can leave an aviator feeling eerily calm. On June 13, 2026, Marine Corps Maj. Jackson Simon emerged from a wooded area with a bloodied face and walked down the road toward a Yakima County sheriff’s deputy, whose bodycam captured the soldier appearing remarkably composed. "I'm a little frazzled," was about as close as Simon came to expressing fear after his F-18 Hornet crashed into the forest and sparked a small wildfire near Rimrock Lake. Buckley, who flew F-18 Hornets during his 15-year career in the U.S. Navy, said Simon was likely experiencing a combination of shock, an adrenaline letdown and the effects of training that teaches pilots to compartmentalize under pressure. EIGHT BELIEVED DEAD AFTER B-52 CRASHES SHORTLY AFTER TAKEOFF FROM EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE "If anything's going wrong, we focus on the task. Everything else goes away," Buckley told Fox News Digital. "That was the most violent thing that ever happened to that Marine in his entire life." Buckley served as a pilot in the Navy from 1991 to 2006 and said he was fortunate never to have ejected from an aircraft. The experience can have a devastating toll on the human body. "Some folks don't go back to flying status. I mean, you can lose a couple inches in height. Your spine compresses. Some people get shorter," Buckley said. A meta-analysis of more than a dozen studies looking at 1,710 military aircrew ejections found a pooled mortality rate of 10.5%, while 29.8% suffered major injuries. The studies were published between 1971 and 2019. ARMY IDENTIFIES 2 PILOTS KILLED IN APACHE HELICOPTER CRASH NEAR FORT HOOD DURING TRAINING EXERCISE "When you pull that handle, you have two choices: die or maybe live. And I said 'maybe live' because it's incredibly violent. I think the average ejection seat is like 10 to 20 G's of force," Buckley added. "Most folks don't even remember the ejection. They remember pulling the handle and then waking up in their parachute." Buckley said the pilot's body positioning before the ejection is extremely important in preventing potentially life-threatening injuries. For example, if their arm is extended away from their body, the sudden wind blast could cause it to be "ripped out of the socket." There's also a phenomenon called "seat slap," which occurs if the pilot does not have their legs flush with the seat prior to ejecting. "If you look at an ejection seat in a fighter jet, it's rock hard. We're not sitting on a cushion," he said. "If your legs aren't flat on the seat, it could break both of your legs and now you bleed out and die." US NAVY IDENTIFIES SAILOR LOST IN ARABIAN SEA AFTER HELICOPTER'S EMERGENCY WATER LANDING In some instances, pilots who find themselves in trouble have time to slow their aircraft and perform a controlled ejection, which can reduce the forces involved, Buckley said. Based on video of the crash, Simon’s plane was traveling at a high rate of speed before it struck the trees and exploded, likely leaving little opportunity for a controlled ejection. Simon had been performing low-flying maneuvers while spectators on the ground watched, according to KIRO 7. After that, his plane reportedly clipped some power lines, which led to it going down. The Marine Corps has not publicly confirmed that Simon’s F-18 struck power lines before the crash and has said the cause of the mishap remains under investigation. UNITED AIRLINES JET FLEW TOO LOW AND TOO SLOW BEFORE STRIKING LIGHT POLE AND TRUCK NEAR NEWARK AIRPORT: NTSB According to Buckley, this "clearly" wasn't supposed to happen. "We have minimum altitude restrictions. And there ain't no 500-foot trees, right? So I don't know what they were doing. It doesn't sound like from his initial statement that there was anything wrong with the airplane. So that's usually not a good sign," Buckley said. Buckley then speculated about what may have been going through Simon’s mind before the crash. "It looked like a beautiful day. People out on a lake. 'Hey, there's some people down there on the lake. Why don't we go show them what their tax money is [for]? You know, America.' I hope it wasn't something like that," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the third Marine Aircraft Wing, the West Coast-based Marine aviation unit to which Simon’s aircraft was assigned. Buckley said Simon will likely go before a review board that will evaluate his actions surrounding the crash. At the conclusion of the process, the board can recommend what should happen to an aviator’s flight status. If he's found to be at fault, Simon could lose his "wings" or he could be allowed to continue flying, just under what Buckley described as "double secret probation." "I don't know what the board's gonna do, but it'll come out. It should because...this is a $60 to $65 million Hornet. We deserve to know what happened," he added.

articles.title: Syria’s economy poised for improvement after US sanctions removal
articles.summary: Removal of US sanctions offers Syria a chance to fully rejoin the global financial system after years of isolation.
articles.body:
Syria’s removal by the United States from its “state sponsors of terrorism” list clears one of the last major hurdles to the country’s integration into the global financial system, analysts tell Al Jazeera.

On July 8, US President Donald Trump announced he was formally notifying Congress of his intention to rescind Syria’s designation, which had been in place since 1979. A 45-day congressional review period passed on Saturday, and the US completed the formal delisting on Monday .

While Washington had already lifted many of the restrictions preventing transactions with Syrian banks, the “terrorism” designation continued to carry additional financial and trade restrictions, and Syria’s removal will give the country – still struggling to pick itself up after a nearly 14-year war – a badly needed economic boost .

“The momentum is great for this announcement, and it was the last main barrier to banks reconnecting [with the global community],” Vittorio Maresca di Serracapriola, sanctions lead analyst for Karam Shaar Advisory, a consulting company with a focus on the political economy of the Middle East, told Al Jazeera.

Syria was first designated by the US as a “state sponsor of terrorism” in 1979 under the presidency of Hafez al-Assad.

The country was originally placed on the list for its support of Palestinian armed groups. Syrian-US relations were later strained when the US invaded Iraq in 2003, just a few years after Hafez died and his son Bashar succeeded him. Washington pulled out of its embassy in Syria in 2012, a year after Syrians rose up against the al-Assad regime, which responded with brutal suppression and violence, leading to war.

During the conflict, Syria became increasingly isolated from the global community as more international sanctions were placed on the regime.

When the al-Assad regime finally collapsed in December 2024, a new government, including members of former rebel groups, took its place. One of its first priorities was trying to reintegrate Syria into the regional and international community by removing the sanctions, which has largely been accomplished .

Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, the former rebel group he led, were also previously under US sanctions, which have been removed .

While Syria has moved on from its isolation since the fall of al-Assad, its economy remains weak with almost 90 percent of the population living below the poverty line.

“For nearly five decades, Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism resulted in severe restrictions on financing and exports and contributed to significant hesitation and overcompliance among banks and investors who were reluctant to engage with Syria, fearing secondary sanctions,” Obai Kurd Ali, a Syrian expert with the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, told Al Jazeera.

“People in Syria are suffering from severe poverty and a deteriorating economic situation with decent living standards becoming unaffordable day after day,” he added. “For Syrians, any step that may lead to better living conditions is worth celebrating, and removing [the] designation is not only one such step but also one of the final major actions toward dismantling the complex web of US sanctions that isolated Syria for so long.”

Maresca di Serracapriola said the decision to lift Syria’s designation reduces legal risks for banks working on Syria-related financing or transactions and allows US foreign assistance to Syria.

“The removal of restrictions on US foreign assistance and government contracting has the potential to open additional channels for development and reconstruction support,” he said, adding that “the biggest impact will likely be on financial flows and investment.”

International banks would often cite the designation as a reason against working with banks in Syria.

“The timing of the announcement is important because the Central Bank of Syria reactivated its account at the Federal Reserve Bank in New York in March, and recently, the World Bank has approved a $100m grant for financial sector modernisation in Syria,” Maresca di Serracapriola said.

Ibrahim Kochaji, a Syrian banking and economic expert, called the lifting of the sanctions “a pivotal moment in the trajectory of the national economy” but said it was “not an immediate remedy” for the country’s deep economic struggles.

Kochaji said any resolution to Syria’s issues requires “a long path of reforms and measures” that would be bolstered by stability and sound governance.

Kurd Ali agreed. “The transitional government must seize this opportunity to put its own house in order,” he said. “Good governance, transparency, robust anticorruption measures and meaningful judicial reform are essential to regain investors’ confidence and ensure that investment contributes to a sustainable and inclusive recovery that puts people’s priorities at its heart.”

The fall of the al-Assad regime was met with jubilation across Syria. And many Syrians still speak about the improvements to their day-to-day lives since the regime’s demise.

But increasingly, Syrians are expressing frustration at the soaring cost of energy and the stuttering local economy.

Kochaji said the removal of sanctions would impact Syrians daily lives but the impact may not be as immediate as some may hope.

“The realistic answer is that the impact will be gradual, but it can become tangible if the government manages the transition wisely,” he said, adding that if managed correctly, production and transportation costs could decrease and new job opportunities could develop, among other potential benefits.

While many of the main economic barriers have been removed, analysts said they believe Syria’s banking sector is not guaranteed to automatically rebound.

“International banks and investors will still look at Syria’s antimoney-laundering and counter-financing of terrorism framework and overall risk environment, also general governance and political stability,” Maresca di Serracapriola said. “So that will not necessarily shift the picture entirely with respect to banking.”

articles.title: Secret Service says it’s aware of Iranian video threatening Barron Trump
articles.summary: The Secret Service on Tuesday said it was aware of a video threatening President Trump’s son, Barron, being circulated by Iranian state media. Clips suggest that Iran’s leaders are tracking Barron’s whereabouts and offering a $10 million reward to those who can provide insight into his location, according to reports from ABC News. “The U.S.…
articles.body:
The Secret Service on Tuesday said it was aware of a video threatening President Trump’s son, Barron, being circulated by Iranian state media.

Clips suggest that Iran’s leaders are tracking Barron’s whereabouts and offering a $10 million reward to those who can provide insight into his location, according to reports from ABC News .

“The U.S. Secret Service is aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees,” Secret Service spokesperson Nate Herring said in a statement to NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network.

“Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence,” Herring added.

In previous instances, Iran has circulated videos and statements threatening to kill the president and his family members. The stakes have heightened as the war in Iran nears the six-month mark with no clear end in sight.

The Trump administration has waged both military and economic war on Tehran and pushed its leaders to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic.

Iran has refused but agreed to work with Oman to open two pathways through the critical waterway for a fee.

Since the U.S. and Israel first struck Iran in February, its leaders have been seeking revenge for the death of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in the strikes.

Iran held a weeklong national ceremony in July to commemorate Khamenei’s life while appointing his son, Mojtaba Khamenei, to serve in his place.

Mojtaba Khamenei was reportedly injured in U.S.-Israeli strikes and has remained absent from direct negotiations with U.S. envoys.

The U.S. and Iran reached a brief ceasefire on June 17 following Pakistan-mediated talks.

President Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed a memorandum of understanding enshrining a 14-point agreement that halted military operations and aimed to reopen the strait.

However, the fragile ceasefire began to break down in early July after renewed vessel attacks in the strait, and the 60-day agreement ultimately expired last week.

articles.title: NYC mom survives neck-slash attack on hiking trip in Arizona: 'I can’t die like this'
articles.summary: Ring camera footage captures New York City mother Alexis Rowan fighting for her life after a stranger slashed her neck on an Arizona birthday hike.
articles.body: A birthday hiking trip of a lifetime wound up being a death-defying fight for her life for a New York City mother of two, leaving her neck slashed, her hand stabbed, as well as physical and emotional scars that left 13 stitches and a nightmare that will never be forgotten. Alexis Rowan, 27, survived the northern Arizona mountain-hike attack only because of screams that were heard by a woman in a nearby home, forcing the suspect to flee, harrowing doorbell camera footage showed. "I was like, oh my God, my neck: I can't die like this, this is not the way," Alexis Rowan told WABC after returning to New York City after last week's ordeal on a tourist mountain hike in Arizona. "I have my kids to go home to." NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING' Graphic photos shared by the New York Post showed the deep slash left on her neck and the 10 stitches that closed it, along with three more from being stabbed in the hand. She never wants "to look at another mountain again," she told the Post, while the lasting scar will remind her of the horror with every look in the mirror. On the Wednesday, Aug. 19, hike at the Havasupai Indian Reservation – just one day after her 27th birthday – Alexis was left briefly behind a friend when the suspect approached. The suspect, identified as Taylor Nardo Paya, 29, is a Havasupai tribe member with a rap sheet that included a guilty plea to assault, according to FOX 10 Phoenix. GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL "It was the first person that I've seen in the village, and I said, 'Hey, excuse me, is that the gift shop?'" Rowan told WABC in one of the few interviews she granted. Fox News Digital reached out to her and her mother for an interview, but they have yet to respond. "I kept walking, I went to go in and that's when he just came up from behind," she continued, "and as soon as I felt my neck, I'm like, 'oh my God, I'm going to die.'" Footage showed Rowan fighting for her life as she was dragged by the hair from the ground – with her screams finally bringing a woman to open the door and causing the suspect to flee. The video obtained by Fox News Digital did not have the sound of the screams, but they were key to the suspect fleeing, according to reports. REPEAT OFFENDER ACCUSED OF COLLEGE STUDENT’S MURDER WAS KNOWN ‘THREAT’ AFTER PRIOR ARREST: VICTIM’S MOM "I'm just so grateful for the woman that opened the door that heard her screams; it's something you can never unhear," Tricia Rowan, Alexis' mother, told WABC of the "angel sent from heaven" woman who opened the door to help. "She's a fighter. She fought to make sure she's coming home to her babies, and she's my baby. So I'm so glad she made it, Tricia Rowan said. "He picked the wrong one. My daughter is a fighter, she is a warrior. She wasn’t going to take it." SENATOR TIM SHEEHY: SOFT-ON-CRIME JUDGES NEED CONSEQUENCES. THE JAIL ACT DELIVERS Alexis Rowan told the Post she was "mentally aware" of the "danger" after her initial interaction with Paya. "My gut instinct was like, ‘This is not OK. I’m not OK,’" she said, adding that the "next person may not be as strong, may not be prepared mentally that someone is going to attack them or able to put them in danger." Reservation police located Paya the following day by pinging Rowan’s phone, which prosecutors say he allegedly stole after it fell from one of her backpacks. WOMAN ALLEGEDLY CHOKED SUBWAY RIDER, YELLED ANTISEMITIC REMARKS IN ATTACK CAUGHT ON VIDEO: POLICE He was arrested and later taken into federal custody because the alleged attack occurred on tribal land, according to reports. Video obtained by Fox News Digital showed Paya being cuffed and taken away on a golf cart by federal police before another video showed him in an orange jumpsuit being perp-walked to a helicopter. Paya faces a federal assault with a deadly weapon charge, according to FOX 10. Court records show Paya pleaded guilty in 2016 to robbing and assaulting another woman in a 2015 attack, for which he received a five-year prison sentence and was ordered to undergo sex offender treatment and counseling. FIVE PLEAD GUILTY TO CHARGES IN BRUTAL CINCINNATI BEATDOWN THAT WENT VIRAL LAST SUMMER The victim's mother wants to see the perpetrator locked up indefinitely. "People are evil," she told the Post, calling him "a threat to society" and someone "you cannot rehabilitate."
