articles.title: 'Shocking' book about Putin's private life wins French literary prize
articles.summary: A taboo-breaking book about Vladimir Putin's rise to power and private life, written by two exiled Russian journalists, won a newly established French litera...
articles.body:
A taboo-breaking book about Vladimir Putin's rise to power and private life, written by two exiled Russian journalists, won a newly established French literary prize on Tuesday.

The book, titled "The Tsar in Propria Persona: How Vladimir Putin Deceived Us All", draws on more than two decades of investigative reporting by journalists Roman Badanin and Mikhail Rubin.

The work won a newly established literary award called the Prix Strasbourg awarded by EBRA, France's largest regional newspaper group, and its parent company, Credit Mutuel Alliance Federale.

The book is due to be published in France next month.

It reads "like a spy novel", the jury said, describing the book as a "fascinating and shocking work about a figure who is himself fascinating and shocking".

"It is the result of several hundred interviews with witnesses, some of whom later disappeared under tragic circumstances."

Badanin is the founder and editor-in-chief of Proekt, an investigative media outlet created in 2018.

Both Badanin and Rubin, his deputy at Proekt, live in the United States after coming under pressure in Russia.

Badanin said the authors wanted foreigners to read the book and learn "actual facts" about Putin and the system he had built.

"The message we wanted to convey with this book is as follows: there is no need to invent anything about Putin. Instead, learn how things really are. That is horrifying enough," he told AFP.

"Only a genuine understanding of the facts can help us make sound assessments, respond effectively, and plan for the future of relations between nations."

When the book's Russian edition was published last year, the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) said that Badanin and Rubin broke a Kremlin-imposed taboo about Putin's private life "at great personal risk".

The book "contrasts the official image of the Russian president, now in his 26th year in power, as a leading defender of traditional values against Western decadence with the reality of his private life -- where extramarital affairs, nepotism, and connections to organised crime reign".

Launched in 2026, the prize seeks to distinguish itself through its substantial endowment, with 20,000 euros ($23,000) awarded to the overall winner and 55,000 euros distributed across all categories.

Other prize winners include Haitian author Thelyson Orelien and French journalist Marion Dubreuil.

articles.title: Democrats push Rubio on Board of Peace ‘slush fund’ for Trump
articles.summary: House Democrats are applying new scrutiny on President Trump’s Board of Peace, demanding answers on how his inner circle is using American tax dollars for a “slush fund” and planning to profit off plans to rebuild the Gaza Strip. The Trump administration was forced to halt the transfer of $50 million to the board in…
articles.body:
House Democrats are applying new scrutiny on President Trump’s Board of Peace, demanding answers on how his inner circle is using American tax dollars for a “slush fund” and planning to profit off plans to rebuild the Gaza Strip.

The Trump administration was forced to halt the transfer of $50 million to the board in July, in the face of pushback from lawmakers who said the State Department could not answer basic questions about the board’s structure, oversight of the funds, and whether Trump could use the funds to compensate himself.

Those questions form the basis of a letter sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday and obtained exclusively by The Hill. The letter also signals that Democrats will open an investigation into Trump’s Board of Peace if they take the majority in the House after the November midterm elections, in which case they would gain subpoena power.

Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking members of the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees, respectively, call for Rubio to answer basic questions about the board’s structure, funding and oversight, nine months after its creation.

“The fact that the Trump Administration, with your help, is attempting to transfer taxpayer dollars to the Board of Peace, an opaque organization primed for corruption, raises serious concerns that public funds could be once again misused by the President and his family and friends,” the lawmakers wrote.

Trump created the Board of Peace in October as part of a plan to end the devastating war between Israel and Hamas in the Gaza Strip, appointing himself as “chairman for life” with apparent unilateral control over the board’s decisions and how money is spent on reconstruction — even beyond his presidency.

The United Nations Security Council endorsed the board until 2027. But in January, Trump expanded the board’s mission to tackle conflict around the world, setting it up to outlive the Security Council deadline. The president solicited billion-dollar pledges from countries in exchange for lifetime membership and promised an initial pledge of $10 billion from the U.S. government.

A Board of Peace official earlier told The Hill that hundreds of millions of dollars have been collected to finance the Gaza peace plan. The Financial Times reported in May that donors preferred placing funds in a bank account managed by J.P. Morgan , rather than the account set up at the World Bank.

Democrats and other critics say there are no clear answers on who is auditing and conducting oversight of the J.P. Morgan account.

On July 29, the State Department notified Congress it was rescinding $50 million in funding it was sending to the Board of Peace from its budget for international organizations and programs.

The notification followed intense pressure from Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, a congressional aide told The Hill. The Board of Peace did not respond to a letter Shaheen sent them in June raising questions about funds, but it has started briefing committee staff, the congressional aide said.

Raskin and Meeks’s letter adds to that pressure. The lawmakers argue that basic questions on whether the Board of Peace is a public or private entity, a U.S. organization or international, or “even a false entity altogether” are unanswered.

“Can anyone assure Congress that billions of dollars from U.S. taxpayers and foreign governments will not be flowing into the pockets of President Trump, members of his family, corrupt and incompetent contractors or business partners, or political allies and foot soldiers of the President?” the lawmakers wrote.

Raskin and Meeks also argue that Trump’s executive order establishing the Board of Peace as a “public international organization” — which would protect it from lawsuits and certain searches from federal law enforcement — is without merit.

A Board of Peace official earlier told The Hill that the board “is an international organization established under international law. Its legal status and mandate derive from the foundational arrangements establishing it and the consent of its participating members.”

But Raskin and Meeks said that such an organization must be established under a treaty or an act of Congress.

“The Board of Peace was created out of thin air and whole cloth by the President, without any input from Congress about any aspect of its operation,” they wrote.

The lawmakers argue that Board of Peace members have been “explicit” about their intention to use it for “private profit-making purposes,” pointing to statements by Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and a board member, advertising “amazing investment opportunities” when promoting the administration’s Gaza plan to the World Economic Forum in Davos in January.

And Raskin further points out that the administration’s goal to trademark Board of Peace earlier this year served as a flashing red light for “backroom deals and procedural illegitimacy.”

Earlier this year, in a move that Raskin described as “almost certainly illegal,” the director of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, John Squires, applied for trademarks on behalf of the board. Squires told Raskin at a Judiciary hearing in March that he filed the trademark to preserve access to the Board of Peace website address in his authority as adviser to the president.

“After Judiciary Committee Democrats demanded information on this trademark application in three oversight letters to Director Squires, he abruptly abandoned the applications but failed to respond to any of our letters or provide information as to who directed him to apply for this trademark for the Board in the first place,” Raskin and Meeks wrote.

The lawmakers gave Rubio a Sept. 8 deadline to answer more than a dozen questions on who manages the Board of Peace, the decisionmaking process, who has the authority to make financial decisions, staffing, what bank accounts are being used and how it’s being overseen, among other questions.

“We will work with you to guarantee the American people full transparency about how their tax dollars are being funneled to — and spent by — this organization never established or authorized by Congress but now poised to receive substantial public funding from the State Department under your direction,” they wrote.

There’s been little progress in finally ending the conflict between Israel and Hamas in Gaza, the narrow seaside territory divided under majority Israeli control but with nearly 2 million Palestinians living under Hamas control. Thousands are displaced, living in bare-bones temporary shelters of tarps or damaged buildings and facing shortages of water, food and medicine.

Last month, the Board of Peace proposed a roadmap to disarm Hamas, and it is pushing Israel to accept the proposal. However, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has shown little interest in finding common ground with Hamas as he fights for his political survival in upcoming elections.

The board is working toward developing a “pilot zone” where tens of thousands of Palestinians could move into reconstructed neighborhoods in southern Gaza free of Hamas control.

articles.title: Nearly 6-foot cobra hiding under kitchen sends India family rushing to safety
articles.summary: Frightened residents may try to trap or kill it instead of calling trained professionals.
articles.body:
A nearly six-foot cobra hiding beneath a kitchen in India sent one family rushing to safety after hissing and movement inside the home revealed a dangerous surprise.

As The Live Nagpur reported , the rescue ended without injury to either the residents or the snake, but the incident showed how quickly a wildlife encounter can become a major safety concern.

At around 2 p.m. on Aug. 11, 2026, the Songade family left their home in Gayatri Colony and alerted neighbors after tracing hissing and movement in the kitchen to a cobra concealed beneath the kitchen area, the publication said.

As neighbors gathered outside, Shubham G.R., president of Wild Animals and Nature Helping Society, was called to the scene. He captured the cobra from the kitchen and released it into the wild, according to TLN.

A venomous cobra inside a home poses a serious risk, especially in a confined indoor space. In India, these types of events crop up from time to time, and it can be alarming for locals.

While it is unclear exactly why this cobra entered the house, situations like this can be linked in part to human activity.

As homes, roads, and neighborhoods expand into or alongside wildlife habitat, animals and people are pushed into closer contact. Even common features around homes, including dark corners, stored belongings, food scraps, and rodents, can make residential spaces appealing hiding spots for snakes.

The BBC has reported that human expansion into natural spaces can increase dangerous encounters with wild animals, creating risks for both residents and animals trying to navigate altered environments.

A cobra in a kitchen can drive a family from their home and cause panic throughout a neighborhood. The situation can also turn deadly for the snake, as frightened residents may try to trap or kill it instead of calling trained professionals.

Instead of trying to deal with the cobra themselves, TLN noted the family kept away from it, alerted others, and sought help from a trained rescuer.

Wildlife rescuers say that is the right response when a snake is found indoors. People should keep their distance, make sure children and pets stay away from the area, and contact an authorized wildlife rescue team or trained snake rescuer as quickly as possible.

Reducing the chances of similar encounters can involve keeping homes and nearby areas clean, limiting places where snakes can hide, and addressing conditions that attract prey animals such as rodents.

Those steps may not eliminate the risk entirely, particularly in places close to wildlife habitat, but they can help reduce the odds of a frightening encounter inside the home.

Fortunately, in this case, the family was unharmed, and the cobra was removed safely, avoiding a much worse outcome.

articles.title: India, China to work towards political settlement of boundary question in long-term interests; Beijing stresses package solution
articles.summary: India News: Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to India next month, India and China held the 25th round of Special Representatives (SR) Dialogue on the.
articles.body: Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to India next month, India and China held the 25th round of Special Representatives (SR) Dialogue on the Boundary Question, endorsing efforts to formalise the recent turnaround in the relationship on the back of border peace and discussing issues like de-escalation, boundary demarcation and border management.After the talks chaired by Special Representatives Ajit Doval and Wang Yi, while India said both sides agreed to work towards a political settlement of the boundary question in their long-term interests, Beijing also recalled a 2005 bilateral agreement to stress its proposal for a package solution.Doval was quoted as saying by the Chinese side that India and China are partners, not competitors, and developing a stable, predictable, and forward-looking India-China relationship carries great significance also for Asia and the world.âThe normalcy we have witnessed in our relationship has been a direct result of both sides maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas,â said Doval, stressing the significance of border peace for further progress in bilateral ties. Wang, however, reiterated Chinaâs position that the border issue must be placed in an âappropriate positionâ in ties.According to a Chinese readout, Doval and Wang held "in-depth communications" on advancing boundary demarcation negotiations, improving border management and control and promoting cross-border cooperation, while reaffirming their commitment to the 2005 agreement on political parameters and guiding principles for a "fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable package settlement" to the boundary question.China had dropped the mention of package settlement, which seeks a quid-pro-quo approach, in its readout of the last round of talks but had used it regularly for SR meetings earlier. Indian governments in the past, like in 2007 in Parliament, have said that they were exploring a "final package settlement" covering all sectors of the boundary under the 2005 bilateral agreement but India has not used that formulation recently, stressing instead on a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable settlement framework.On this occasion, the Indian government said in a statement that under the strategic guidance of PM Narendra Modi and President Xi, - in a constructive and forward-looking spirit â Doval and Wang had a candid exchange of views and agreed to continue their work in seeking a "political settlement of the boundary question in the context of their overall and long-term interests".The SR talks took place ahead of likely back-to-back bilateral meeting between Modi and Xi - first in Kyrgyzstan on the margins of the upcoming SCO summit and second at the BRICS summit that India will host on September 12-13. Xi is expected to arrive in India on September 12 for his first visit to the country in 7 years. While the schedule is yet to be confirmed, official sources said he will have a bilateral meeting with Modi and attend the PM's welcome dinner for BRICS leaders on September 12, before participating in the BRICS summit the next day.On the boundary issue, the Chinese side further said that both countries agreed to properly handle the boundary question through dialogue and consultation, jointly safeguarding peace and tranquility in the border areas.According to Beijing, Wang said that China-India relations have surpassed the bilateral scope and hold global and strategic significance and pointed to consensus reached in Modi-Xi metings in Kazan and Tianjin."China is willing to join hands with India to grasp bilateral relations from a strategic height and long-term perspective, strengthen communication, enhance understanding, resolve differences, overcome obstacles, and serve as good neighbors, friends, and mutually enabling partners, thereby realizing the vision of the Dragon-Elephant Tango," said Wang.Doval also called on Chinese Vice-President Han Zheng during the visit and discussed ways to strengthen peace and tranquility in the border areas and further improve bilateral relations across economic, political and multilateral forums.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Liberia's ex-vice president will await trial on drug trafficking and other charges in prison
articles.summary: Liberia's former vice president was sent to prison on Tuesday to await trial on drug trafficking and other charges, after a court in the West African country...
articles.body:
MONROVIA, Liberia (AP) — Liberia's former vice president was sent to prison on Tuesday to await trial on drug trafficking and other charges, after a court in the West African country denied her request to be released on humanitarian grounds for medical treatment.

Jewel Howard-Taylor's lawyers asked the court for her to remain at a local hospital in Monrovia to receive treatment for a health emergency. She suffered an asthma attack and her blood pressure was high while in police custody after her arrest, according to local media reports.

Alongside three other foreign nationals charged in absentia, the former vice president and wife of former president, Charles Taylor, is facing multiple charges for drug trafficking, money laundering and other offenses as part of an investigation into an alleged transnational narcotics network. Howard-Taylor was vice president from 2018 to 2024.

She was arrested on Aug. 19 at Roberts International Airport while she was attempting to leave Liberia.

Her lawyers have rejected the allegations, saying they are politically motivated, but investigators say the case is supported by travel records, audio recordings, witness testimonies and evidence of her alleged association with members of the transnational cocaine trafficking network.

Last month, Liberian authorities seized and burned around 4.2 metric tons of cocaine with a street value estimated to be about $317 million, also implicating some senior police officials in the trafficking operation, which has been linked to her.

In recent years, West Africa has emerged as a key transit route for cocaine trafficked from South America to Europe, with smugglers taking advantage of porous borders and weak enforcement in parts of the region.

articles.title: Ukrainians seeking beauty in a bomb-scarred city
articles.summary: The Ukrainian city of Izyum has been splintered by Russian bombs -- but 21-year-old Violetta Dezhyna's job is to find beauty in those broken places and help...
articles.body:
The Ukrainian city of Izyum has been splintered by Russian bombs -- but 21-year-old Violetta Dezhyna's job is to find beauty in those broken places and help keep the city alive, even as Russia advances once more.

In dusty streets teeming with men in camouflage and scattered with wrecked military vehicles she scours for scenes of normality to post on the city social media pages.

Pruned flowerbeds stand in front of gutted and mangled apartment blocks.

"Here the buildings are destroyed, not pretty. Here, it seems, there's a fountain, but on the other side there's a ruined building," said Dezhyna, who works for the local admimistration.

"I try to find angles where those things aren't visible."

Russia's army captured Izyum, the gateway to Ukraine's eastern Donbas region -- a key target for Russian President Vladimir Putin -- at the start of its 2022 invasion, occupying it for six months before Ukraine retook control.

The majority of Izyum's pre-invasion population of 45,000 came back after Russian troops were pushed back some 60 kilometres (36 miles) in a lightning Ukrainian counter-offensive in autumn 2022.

Dezhyna, then a teenager, returned with her family to help "rebuild" the wounded city.

But the battles have left deep scars on Izyum and its residents -- both physical and psychological.

Months of grinding advances have brought the Russian troops to within 30 kilometres (18 miles) of Izyum again.

And Dezhyna is watching many of her young friends leave once more.

To be around people and feel a sense of community, she frequents the local gym.

Hidden in the basement of a supermarket, the thick smell of sweat hangs heavy in the air as she pushes weights alongside bearded muscle-men.

In between sets, she chats casually with soldiers and their wives -- many more than twice her age.

Over the echo of nearby explosions, they sometimes play beach volleyball near the river -- "the most beautiful place in town".

Back in the office, cracks in the walls and aluminium tape over the windows -- to stop glass shards flying into the building in case of an explosion -- reveal the constant danger faced by those in the city.

Another worker -- also a young women, with blue hair -- took out a small mirror, applied lip gloss then lifted her eyes to the window: taking in the sight of anti-drone nets that engulf the city's buildings and roads.

In another official building across town, violin notes mixed with air raid sirens.

Tamara Georgina, 58, was preparing the room for an upcoming wedding.

"This is resistance ... to spite the enemy. We work, we live, we show that we're not surrendering. This is our town and we're rebuilding it," she told AFP.

Behind her the groom, a soldier, quickly answered his phone.

Residents say many buildings in the city are "marked" -- a term meaning they are a known target for the Russian army.

They include many places where young people typically gather, like the city's Palace of Culture.

Some still kill time in the ruins of what was once a city landmark -- vaping amid the smell of urine.

Dezhyna, who leaves a faint floral scent behind her as she paces the streets, is lobbying officials to rebuild a skate park.

If young people leave, "there will be no future at all," she said.

"I want our community to thrive. I don't want it to remain ... grey."

Roughly 2,000 children still live in Izyum.

School activities -- transformed by the war into classes such as "emotional resilience" -- take place in the building's basement.

Classes for Dezhyna -- then in her final year -- were cancelled on February 24, 2022, the day Russia invaded.

Her prom dress was supposed to arrive the next day.

"I can't say the feelings are very good," she said, walking through her old classroom, chairs now covered in dust.

Russian troops had used it as a base during their occupation of the city.

With them inching closer to the city, Dezhyna and her parents are again thinking about whether they should flee to refuge, far from her beloved Izyum.

"We have to think about it, but I don't want to," she said.

articles.title: Spanish government says sorry to people of Ceuta for migrant crisis
articles.summary: Several thousand migrants remain in the enclave after a mass crossing from Morocco in late July.
articles.body:
The Spanish government has apologised to the people of Ceuta for the migrant crisis that has affected the city for weeks and it has unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws.

"I want to apologise to all those who may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared for," Defence Minister Margarita Robles told a parliamentary committee.

"I have witnessed first-hand your feelings of anxiety, of abandonment, of lack of safety."

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa on 30 and 31 July.

Most of the migrants swam around the border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas.

The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most sleeping rough on beaches or streets.

The Socialist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has been under mounting pressure to resolve the situation, with many residents and the local authorities in Ceuta, which has a population of 84,000, complaining that it is unsustainable.

The Sánchez government has now declared a situation of interest for national security in the city, centralising management of the crisis. Territorial Policy Minister Ángel Víctor Torres has been tasked with co-ordinating the response, relieving the Ceuta local government of that responsibility.

Coinciding with the government's moves and Robles's parliamentary appearance – the first by ministers on this issue over the coming days – changes were also announced to migration and asylum legislation.

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said the reforms would seek to ensure Spain that was fully in line with new EU regulations and that its process was "orderly, efficient, and... [provided] all possible guarantees".

It will include limiting to three days the amount of time an undocumented migrant can spend undergoing medical, biometric and legal evaluation on arrival – EU regulations allow this period to last up to seven days.

The reforms will also create a two-speed system for processing asylum requests, in theory accelerating cases deemed urgent.

However, the information provided by government ministers has left some questions unanswered.

Robles told parliament that agents of the CNI intelligence service had shared information about a possible imminent migrant crossing with security forces shortly before it happened, but Grande-Marlaska appeared to contradict her.

"There was no report that hinted that on 30 July what eventually happened was going to happen," he said. Robles later said that the information had not been conveyed via a report.

Sánchez has blamed traffickers and social media activity for the mass crossing.

However, many others have pointed the finger at Morocco, which in the past has been accused of using the borders with Ceuta and its sister city Melilla to pressure Madrid or the EU on political issues.

"The crisis in Ceuta didn't begin on 30 July," said Esther Muñoz of the conservative People's Party (PP), as she questioned Robles in parliament.

"It's been brewing for years and you know it, because you know that [the Moroccan authorities] have spent years sizing us up, sizing up our ability to respond and our willingness to do so."

The crisis has raised concerns in Spain about Moroccan claims to Ceuta and Melilla.

Last week, Moroccan Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi spoke of his country's "historical and geographical right" to the cities and proposed talks with Spain on the issue.

Robles told the parliamentary committee she not would not allow "any minister from any government, in this case Morocco, to question the Spanish status of Ceuta and Melilla".

articles.title: Kurdish-led forces in Syria dissolve after merging with army
articles.summary: Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) commander campaigns for Kurdish language preservation after decade fighting ISIL.
articles.body:
The head of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), which spearheaded the fight in Syria against the ISIL (ISIS) armed group, has announced its dissolution as part of a deal struck with the government in Damascus.

"We announce today the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces and declare, with full responsibility, their dissolution as an independent military force," Mazloum Abdi said on Tuesday evening in a televised speech at the presidential palace in Damascus.

The SDF once controlled a de facto autonomous zone in Syria's northeast. Abdi said the group has completed a merger with the Syrian army and would cease to operate as an independent force.

The Kurdish-led force lost most of its territory in northeastern Syria in January during a government offensive and then signed the deal to merge with the army.

The SDF was once the main partner of the United States in Syria as it battled ISIL. But after the ouster of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, Washington formed close ties with the new government in Damascus, led by interim Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, the leader of the opposition forces that overthrew al-Assad.

"Today we stand at a historic moment in which we turn an important page in Syria's history and begin to open a new page titled peace, stability and reconstruction," Abdi was quoted as saying by the state news agency, SANA.

"We want this day to be the beginning of a true transition from the battlefields to the fields of construction and from the era of weapons to the era of peace," he added.

On a cultural note, Abdi said al-Sharaa has recognised the "preservation of our right to education in the Kurdish language", adding that they would work to implement "education in the Kurdish language during the current year".

"We want to build a new Syria for all its people – the Kurds, Arabs, Turkmen and Assyrians – a unified and stable Syria that protects the future of its children and ensures a dignified life for its youth," he said, according to SANA.

United States Ambassador to Turkiye and Special Envoy for Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, lauded President Trump's "far-sighted leadership [that] opened the path for the SDF's orderly integration into Syrian state institutions."

"Recognizing the Kurdish language in education and securing substantive roles for our valued partners Mazloum Abdi and Ilham Ahmed within the Syrian government pays due respect to their leadership, the sacrifices of our Kurdish partners, and the constructive contribution they have made to regional stability—turning yesterday's separations into tomorrow's shared purpose," Barrack wrote in a post on X.

Abdi's announcement came a day after the US removed Syria from its "state sponsors of terrorism" list, a decades-old designation that came with severe economic restrictions. It marked another step in closer ties between the two countries after the ouster of al-Assad.

Al-Sharaa hailed the move, saying, "Syria shakes off a dark stain and tears away a painful chapter of its past to embark on a path of development, reconstruction and rebuilding."

articles.title: Dolly Parton y la pérdida de la que nunca pudo recuperarse: "no hay palabras que describan nuestro amor"
articles.summary: Siempre sonriente y llena de energía. Esa es la imagen que, durante más de medio siglo, Dolly Parton decidió mostrarle a sus fanáticos y el mundo entero. Sin...
articles.body:
Siempre sonriente y llena de energía . Esa es la imagen que, durante más de medio siglo, Dolly Parton decidió mostrarle a sus fanáticos y el mundo entero. Sin embargo, en marzo de 2025 la célebre cantante -que murió este martes, a los 80 años - recurrió a sus redes sociales para informar la más triste de las noticias: la pérdida de Carl Dean, su marido y el hombre con el que había compartido las últimas seis décadas de su vida.

En el texto que se había compartido el 3 de marzo del año pasado a su cuenta de Instagram, se indicó: "Carl Dean, el esposo de Dolly Parton, falleció el 3 de marzo en Nashville a la edad de 82 años. Será enterrado en una ceremonia privada a la que asistirá su familia inmediata. Le sobreviven sus hermanos Sandra y Donnie".

El comunicado, además, incluía una declaración de Parton: " Carl y yo pasamos muchos años maravillosos juntos. Las palabras no pueden hacer justicia al amor que compartimos durante más de 60 años . Gracias por sus oraciones y su empatía".

La gran historia de amor entre Parton y Dean nació en las sombras. De mundos totalmente opuestos (a ella le fascinaba el glamour, la purpurina y las luces de Hollywood, mientras que él era un chico sencillo y de bajo perfil que huía del foco mediático), los tortolitos se cruzaron de casualidad y se enamoraron perdidamente . Y si bien su historia de amor siempre estuvo catalogada como una de las más románticas del ambiente, lo cierto es que al principio la relación no fue nada fácil: la pareja tuvo que ocultarse durante un largo tiempo y hasta casarse en secreto debido a ciertas cláusulas del sello discográfico que manejaba la carrera de la cantante por aquel entonces.

Nacida el 19 de enero de 1946 en Sevierville, Tennessee, Dolly Rebecca Parton terminó el secundario y se mudó a Nashville para cumplir su sueño de convertirse en una estrella de la música country. El encuentro se produjo de pura casualidad afuera de la lavandería Wishy Washy. "He venido a Nashville con ropa sucia, tenía tanta prisa por llegar aquí. Después de poner mi ropa en la máquina, empecé a caminar por la calle y este tipo me gritó desde su camioneta. Yo saludé. Al ser del campo, hablaba con todo el mundo", recordaba, entre risas, la compositora de "Jolene" sobre el día que se cruzó por primera vez a su marido.

El flechazo fue tan fuerte que Parton reconocía haber sentido una conexión instantánea desde un primer momento. " Estaba sorprendida y encantada de que mientras me hablaba, me miraba a la cara, una cosa rara para mí. Parecía estar genuinamente interesado en descubrir quién era yo y de qué iba ", confesaba sobre qué fue lo que más la atrapó de este misterioso hombre.

Y aunque la historia empezó de una manera un tanto extraña, la joven recién llegada del pueblo no quiso perderse la oportunidad de vivirla. "No es frecuente que alguien pueda decir que su vida cambió para siempre en un lugar llamado Wishy Washy. Acababa de graduarme de la secundaria, había dejado dos novios en casa y no tenía intenciones de encontrar otro. Sólo quería trabajar en mi música. No quería que ningún chico, ningún hombre, ni nadie me desviara. Entonces, ¿qué estaba haciendo el primer día?", se cuestionó, aunque inmediatamente lo invitó a la casa de sus tíos, donde ella se alojaba.

"Mi primer pensamiento fue: 'Me voy a casar con esa chica'. El segundo fue: 'Señor, ella es guapa'. Y ese fue el día en que comenzó mi vida. No cambiaría los últimos 50 años por nada en esta tierra", reveló en una entrevista el hombre que -tras visitarla todos los días durante una semana- la invitó a una primera cita oficial. "Él quería llevarme a cenar. Se detuvo en la ventanilla del autocine y compró nuestra comida en McDonald's", revelaba la actriz con un dejo de nostalgia, en 2018.

Poco después de comenzar su relación, Dean se alistó en el ejército, pero ellos se mantuvieron en contacto durante sus dos años de servicio. A su regreso, los enamorados decidieron casarse, a lo que Monument, el sello discográfico que manejaba la carrera de la artista por aquellos años, se opuso rotundamente. Al parecer, los productores temían que su matrimonio afectara negativamente su profesión. "Todos en mi sello habían invertido dinero en mí y en la construcción de mi carrera, por lo que me preguntaron si esperaría un año para casarme (…). Yo no tenía la intención de encontrar a nadie, pero ya sabes cómo va el amor", contó confirmando los rumores.

Mujer de armas tomar, Parton desoyó el pedido de los empresarios y se escapó junto a su novio para sellar su amor del otro lado de la frontera. El 30 de mayo de 1966, la pareja se casó en secreto en una capilla de Ringgold, Georgia, a la que solo asistieron la madre de Dolly, Avie Lee, el pastor Don Duvall y su esposa. "Fuimos ese mismo fin de semana a una pequeña iglesia en Ringgold. Tenía un simple vestido blanco y poquitas flores, y mi madre se fue conmigo", recordó la estrella estadounidense sobre uno de los días más importantes de su vida.

Durante más de un año, la pareja ocultó su matrimonio. Evitaban ser vistos en público y propiciar cualquier rumor que los pudiera unir. Será por eso que cuando finalmente decidieron decir la verdad, nadie podía creerlo. Contra todos los pronósticos, la carrera de Parton despegó a escalas inimaginables, no sólo convirtiéndose en "la reina del country" sino en una de las actrices más convocadas de la pantalla grande.

A pesar de estar casado con una de las máximas referentes del cine, la música y la televisión de la época, Carl Dean siempre dejó en claro que quería mantenerse alejado del estilo de vida de una celebridad. "Te amo y te apoyaré en tu carrera de cualquier manera que pueda, pero nunca me pidas que vaya a otra de esas malditas cosas otra vez", le advirtió el director de una compañía de pavimentación a su mujer después de asistir a una entrega de premios.

Dicen que "los opuestos se atraen" y en este caso esa premisa encajó a la perfección. " Somos completamente opuestos pero eso es lo que lo hace divertido. Nunca sé lo que va a decir o a hacer. Siempre me sorprende ", confesó la protagonista de Cómo eliminar a su jefe dando cuenta de que es lo que más la atrapa de su hombre. En cuanto a cómo toma su sencillez y bajo perfil, la nominada 47 veces a los Grammy expresó: "Mi marido es solitario. Siempre me ha pedido que lo deje fuera de todo esto. No le gusta el alboroto".

Es así como, desde el primer día que se conocieron, este matrimonio decidió construir su intimidad lejos de los flashes. "Nos gusta meternos en nuestra pequeña burbuja y ser simples. A mí me encanta leer, cocinar, estar con mi marido. Me pongo mi ropa cómoda (la llamo mi ropa de bebé) y simplemente nos relajamos (…). Me casé con un hombre realmente bueno, un tipo que es completamente diferente a mí. Le encanta escuchar sobre las cosas que hago. Me encanta escuchar sobre las cosas que hace. Así que disfrutamos de la compañía del otro. Nos llevamos bien", aseguró.

Al parecer, esta fórmula les funcionó a la perfección durante los 60 años que permanecieron juntos. "Él es como un hermano, un padre, un amigo, un marido y un amante para mí (…). Nos gustamos, nos respetamos, siempre lo hemos pasado bien", reconoció durante una aparición en Good Morning Britain .

El amor entre ellos fue tan grande que, con motivo de su 50 aniversario, la pareja decidió renovar sus votos matrimoniales el 30 de mayo de 2016. "Voy a tener un hermoso vestido de novia porque no tuve uno grande y largo cuando nos casamos y tenemos un traje para él, así que vamos a vestirnos y a tomar un montón de fotos", reveló mientras organizaba una celebración totalmente diferente a la primera boda.

Sin embargo, no todo fue un lecho de rosas y a lo largo del tiempo la pareja debió afrontar ciertas situaciones conflictivas. Los primeros rumores sobre una posible infidelidad surgieron en 1973, cuando Dolly lanzó su exitosa canción "Jolene". La letra de la pegadiza melodía -que describe a una hermosa y joven mujer pelirroja llamada Jolene- inmediatamente desató dudas sobre una posible relación extramatrimonial de su esposo Carl.

Lejos de desmentir estas versiones, la propia compositora usó este "mito" para jugar en sus shows a través de comentarios como "le prohibí a Carl que fuera al banco donde trabaja Jolene", algo que el público recibía con mucha gracia. Sin embargo, en los últimos años la dueña de Dollywood (un parque temático donde solía hacer sus conciertos) decidió desestimar el rumor y reveló una inspiración mucho menos escandalosa para la famosa canción. Según The Independent, Jolene es en realidad una niña que la artista conoció en uno de sus shows y prometió escribir una canción sobre ella, porque tenía "el nombre más bonito" que había escuchado.

Ahora bien, Dean no fue el único señalado como infiel. Luego de que la escritora confesara en su libro Dolly on Dolly: Interviews and Encounters With Dolly Parton que su matrimonio era "totalmente abierto" , las especulaciones sobre un affaire que la devastó por completo se pusieron en marcha. "Lloré un océano pero no voy a hablar más de ello. Tengo que mantener un poco de misterio", lanzó sin revelar la identidad del supuesto amante.

A pesar de la solidez de la relación, otro hecho llamó siempre la atención de la prensa y los seguidores de la diva estadounidense: ¿por qué no tuvieron hijos? "Dios tiene un plan para todo", repetía casi como un mantra cada vez que le preguntaban por sus ganas de ampliar la familia. Sin embargo, con el tiempo Parton logró entender el motivo por el cual nunca se convirtió en madre . "Al principio, cuando mi marido y yo estábamos saliendo (y luego cuando nos casamos), supusimos que tendríamos hijos. No estábamos haciendo nada para detenerlo. Incluso hasta teníamos los nombres, pero no resultó. Ahora pienso que Dios no quiso que tuviera hijos para que los hijos de todos pudieran ser míos", reflexionó, quien ha logrado acercarse a los más pequeñitos desde su costado solidario.

"Siempre bromeo y me río cuando la gente me pregunta cuál es la clave de mi largo matrimonio. Yo siempre digo: '¡No estén pegoteados!' y hay mucha verdad en eso. Yo viajo mucho, pero realmente disfrutamos el uno del otro cuando estamos juntos y las pequeñas cosas que hacemos ", señalaba Parton. "Él está loco y yo estoy loca. Nos reímos mucho y creo que esa ha sido una de las partes más preciosas de nuestra relación (…). Pero, sobre todo, tienes que respetarte y gustarte, perdonar muchas cosas y aceptar muchas otras", le confesaba la diva a US Weekly.

Días después de dar a conocer la triste noticia de la muerte de su esposo, la cantante, actriz, compositora y empresaria escribió en su cuenta de Instagram: "Me enamoré de Carl Dean cuando tenía 18 años. Hemos pasado 60 años preciosos y significativos juntos. Como todas las grandes historias de amor, nunca terminan. Viven en el recuerdo y en las canciones . Él siempre será la estrella de la historia de mi vida y le dedico esta canción 'If You Hadn't Been There' ".

"Si no hubieras estado ahí... ¿Dónde estaría yo? Sin tu confianza, amor y comprensión... Los altibajos siempre los hemos compartido, y yo no estaría aquí si no hubieras estado ahí", rezaba la letra del tema que Parton le dedicó a su difunto esposo.

En otra estrofa de la canción, Parton expresaba: "Siempre ves lo mejor en mí. Tus brazos amorosos me han acunado, me sostuviste cerca, y creo que no estaría aquí si no hubieses estado ahí, sosteniendo mi mano, mostrándome que te importo. Me hiciste soñar más de lo que me atrevía".

"Eres mi roca; un lugar suave para aterrizar. Mis alas, mi confianza", continúa la letra del tema. Y finaliza: "No estaría aquí si tú no hubieras estado ahí, empujándome. Cuando tenía miedo, encontré a Dios y a ti. Por tu cuidado amoroso y por darme amor de sobra, me hiciste subir y subir las escaleras. No estaría aquí si tú no hubieras estado ahí".

Desde ese duro golpe, y pese a sus ganas de seguir adelante, la salud de Dolly Parton fue en picada. En septiembre del año pasado, anunció la cancelación de su primera residencia en Las Vegas en 32 años debido a "problemas de salud". La cantante tenía previsto ofrecer seis conciertos en The Colosseum del Caesars Palace en diciembre. "No se preocupen, no dejé el negocio porque Dios todavía no ha dicho nada de parar. Pero creo que me está diciendo que baje el ritmo ahora mismo para poder estar lista para más grandes aventuras con todos ustedes" dijo ella en ese momento.

"Tenía un cálculo renal que me estaba causando muchos problemas; resultó que me había provocado una infección, y el médico dijo: 'No necesitás estar viajando en este momento, así que necesitas unos días para mejorar'", señaló. En octubre, Parton publicó un video en redes sociales bromeando con que "todavía no se había muerto", tras varias especulaciones sobre su salud.

"Hay muchos rumores circulando. Pero pensé que si lo escuchaban de mí, sabrían que estaba bien", dijo en un video de dos minutos publicado en su cuenta de Instagram. " Todavía no estoy lista para morir. No creo que Dios haya terminado conmigo. Y yo no he terminado de trabajar ".

En mayo de este año volvió a cancelar sus shows en Las Vegas. "La buena noticia es que estoy respondiendo muy bien a los medicamentos y tratamientos y estoy mejorando cada día", dijo en esa ocasión. "Ahora, la mala noticia es que me va a tomar un poco de tiempo antes de estar al nivel para actuar en el escenario, porque algunos de los medicamentos y tratamientos me dejan un poquito con la cabeza dando vueltas, como solía decir mi abuela".

"Y, por supuesto, no puedo estar mareada cargando banjos, guitarras y esas cosas con tacones, y ustedes saben que voy a estar usándolos. Sin mencionar todos esos atuendos pesados con pedrería, el gran peinado, mi gran… eh, personalidad. ¡Dios mío, eso, eso le daría vueltas la cabeza a cualquiera!".

articles.title: Syria's Kurdish-led SDF dissolves as part of integration with Damascus
articles.summary: DAMASCUS, Aug 25 (Reuters) - The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces has been dissolved, the armed militant group's leader said on Tuesday, a major step in...
articles.body:
SDF commander Mazloum Abdi delivers a speech during a celebration marking the centenary of the city of Qamishli

DAMASCUS, Aug 25 (Reuters) - The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces has been dissolved, the armed militant group's leader said ‌on Tuesday, a major step in the integration plan ‌agreed on earlier this year with the Islamist-led government in Damascus.

"We announce ​today the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces and announce with full responsibility its dissolution as an independent military force," SDF commander Mazloum Abdi said in a televised speech.

The ‌government and the ⁠group, which helped defeat the Islamic State with U.S. backing and held parts of northern and ⁠eastern Syria, agreed in January to a phased integration of Kurdish fighters into the state, a plan Washington called a "historic milestone".

The ​deal came ​shortly after government forces under ​President Ahmed al-Sharaa launched a ‌lightning offensive in January, taking swathes of the areas the SDF held.

Abdi said that the announcement followed an agreement with Sharaa after the integration of the group's forces into the army.

The Kurdish People's Protection Units, which formed the core of ‌the SDF, had already been integrated ​within state forces with its commander, ​Sipan Hamo, appointed in ​March deputy defence minister for the country's eastern ‌territories.

The SDF dissolution comes as the ​new leaders ​in Damascus seek to resolve internal strife and rebuild Syria, with support from Washington, after nearly 14 years of ​civil war and ‌decades of isolation under former President Bashar al-Assad's rule.

(Reporting ​by Orhan Qereman and Nayera Abdallah, Writing by Nayera ​Abdallah; Editing by Alistair Bell)

articles.title: China hits out at 'illegal' new US sanctions on Iran and trading partners
articles.summary: The US has threatened to isolate nations that continue to do business with Tehran, which sells much of its oil to Beijing.
articles.body:
Watch: What are these sanctions and who will be affected?

China has vowed to protect its interests after the US announced plans to widen economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, which include Beijing.

Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.

This came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the new measures on Monday, warning any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, although the trade has declined under the US blockade of Iran's ports.

Lin said: "Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted."

Bessent described the plans for sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever" against Iran, warning banks and businesses would share in Iran's isolation if they refused to cut ties with the country.

He declined to focus on specific nations, but said US President Donald Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime".

However, responding to a question about Chinese banks, Bessent said he wanted to make clear "no one was above the reach of US sanctions".

The announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.

Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.

Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.

China's response followed Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh saying Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he said would lead to "another defeat" for the US.

"The government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television.

"We also have our own tools and know how to play the game," he said, adding Tehran had been "waiting for these plans for a long time".

Iran says it is 'fully prepared' to counter widened US economic sanctions

The US has dubbed its latest sanctions "Operation Economic Outcast" and described them as an "economic D-Day" against Iran.

It comes almost six months after the start of the Iran war.

The conflict has since led to hikes in oil prices worldwide, with Tehran effectively blocking exports through the Strait of Hormuz - a waterway vital to the global economy. The US has also slowed traffic via its own naval blockade.

Recent attempts to end the conflict via diplomacy have failed, and a 60-day ceasefire formally expired last week with no sign of a settlement.

With the announcement of new sanctions, the US treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it".

UK Chancellor John Healey said the British government supported "US work to secure a diplomatic solution and welcome efforts to increase pressure".

Iran is already under heavy sanctions from the US, but Bessent said these go further.

He said the Treasury had mapped financial channels, facilitators and networks used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil, imposing sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels.

But analysts had cast doubt on the latest measures even before China's response.

David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told the BBC the direct impact on Iran's energy revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib".

"We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term," he added.

This is partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, he said, "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either".

Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group, said: "Generally, the Chinese are against unilateral sanctions. They would comply with multilateral or international sanctions, but unilateral sanctions just imposed by the US - they have always seen that as illegitimate."

And although Iran's neighbours like Pakistan, Turkey and Iraq want to maintain good relationships with the US, they "can't really afford to cut off ties with Iran", Vaez told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He said putting economic pressure on Tehran "doesn't work" because the Iranian regime is willing to "absorb any pain" and pass it onto the people.

Other trade partners that could be affected by the US announcement include India and Russia, who have not yet responded.

articles.title: Canada’s minister of industry: ‘We’ll always call it Lake Ontario’
articles.summary: Mélanie Joly, Canada’s minister of industry, rebuffed President Trump’s warning to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Tuesday, saying Canadians will “always call it Lake Ontario.” “We’re proud of our Great Lakes,” Joly told reporters during a Tuesday press conference. “We’ve navigated the St. Lawrence River, the Great Lakes, for thousands of years, and it…
articles.body:
Mélanie Joly, Canada’s minister of industry, rebuffed President Trump’s warning to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Tuesday, saying Canadians will “always call it Lake Ontario.”

“We’re proud of our Great Lakes,” Joly told reporters during a Tuesday press conference. “We’ve navigated the St. Lawrence River, the Great Lakes, for thousands of years, and it was part of a foundation of our country. And we’ll just stand up for what we have.”

Met with applause, Joly added that while “all these shenanigans are happening” — referring to the president’s ongoing trade war with Canada — “we’ll just be smart and we’ll be strategic and we’ll fight back.”

Trump’s warning resembles his 2025 executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the “ Gulf of America ” — a move he described at the time as retaliation against the U.S.’s southern neighbor for “allowing millions of people to pour into our country.”

On Instagram, the official White House account shared a photo of a U.S. map appearing as though it was built using Legos. Above the Great Lakes region appears a rectangle containing the words “Lake America,” while the southern gulf has a similar sign that reads “Gulf of America.”

The renewed trade war between Washington and Ottawa began after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney removed negotiators from trade talks with the U.S. over the weekend, causing a new set of tariffs on several Canadian goods to go into effect.

Carney then announced that, starting Sept. 8, Ottawa would enact retaliatory tariffs in response to the U.S.’s 50 percent tariffs . He told reporters that it would “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

François-Philippe Champagne, Canada’s minister of finance, said Tuesday that Canada will impose 15 percent, 25 percent and 50 percent tariffs on $27.6 billion of U.S. goods. Canada is doubling its tariffs on U.S. steel and aluminum to 50 percent — exactly matching the U.S.’s rate.

“For each product, our tariff will match the American tariff on the same type of Canadian good,” Champagne said.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford preceded Joly in clapping back at Trump’s warning, telling CNN on Tuesday that the threats were a “lot of rhetoric.”

“We’re strong believers in being a sovereign country, and when President Trump wants to attack our sovereignty and attack our businesses and people in Ontario, I can’t roll over,” he told the network’s Wolf Blitzer. “My job is to protect Ontario and Canada, and ironically, protecting the American people.”

The Ontario premier called on both sides of the fight to bring down the temperature, telling Blitzer that “things got a little heated” between him and Trump.

“Let’s negotiate a fair deal because it’s hurting the U.S. It’s hurting Canada, and we just want to make sure that we have a fair deal,” Ford said.

articles.title: More than 50 kidnapped after violent gang attack in Haiti leaves 47 dead
articles.summary: It is believed to be one of the largest mass kidnappings in Haiti in recent years, and one gang leader is threatening to kill the hostages.
articles.body: PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti — At least 47 people were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped after armed men attacked a once-peaceful community near Haiti’s capital earlier this week, the United Nations said Tuesday. It is believed to be one of the largest mass kidnappings in Haiti in recent years, and one gang leader is threatening to kill the hostages if authorities kill any gang members as they try to secure the community nestled in the hills above Port-au-Prince. Sunday’s attack on Kenscoff pierced the belief that security in the troubled Caribbean country was improving. “This is a major political and security test, for the government, for the police and for the international mission alike,” said Romain Le Cour, head of Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime. He said the threat of executing hostages is a trap: If forces don’t act, they’ve failed to protect them; if they do and hostages die, the gangs will blame the state. A threat posted on social media In a video posted on social media, the gang leader threatened Vladimir Paraison, director of Haiti’s National Police. “Paraison, if any of our soldiers are hurt, I will kill all of them,” he said, referring to the hostages. The gang member identified himself as Izo 2, a reference to Izo, or Johnson André, one of Haiti’s most powerful gang leaders. Le Cour said Izo 2 is also known as “Didi” and leads the armed group in Kenscoff on behalf of and in coordination with Izo and other gang leaders. He said the aim of Sunday’s attack could be to force Haiti’s police and the U.N.-backed gang suppression force to disperse even more of their limited resources. “They don’t have enough personnel,” Le Cour said in a phone interview. “If you force them to deploy more troops, it would inevitably be at the expense of other areas.” The attack might also just be a show of force and a message to Haiti’s government and police as the country prepares to hold general elections on Dec. 13 for the first time in more than a decade. “This is a message to the government and the police that their claims of protection do not match reality,” Le Cour said. “The gangs are saying: When we choose to attack, we can, and we will succeed.” Attacks on Kenscoff have escalated The first major attack on Kenscoff occurred in January 2025, and since then, there have been sporadic attacks in the mountains surrounding the city center. But Sunday’s attack was the largest yet. At least five of the 47 people killed were children, according to the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti, known as BINUH. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack on Tuesday, noting that 22 of the victims were reportedly executed in a church compound where they had sought shelter: “The relentless gang attacks on communities and the loss of lives underscore the alarming security conditions in Haiti.” Kenscoff Mayor Jean Massillon told The Associated Press on Tuesday that gangs set fire to 25 homes and killed two government employees, including his cousin, who served as his security detail. “The atrocity of this crime reminds us that we have to continue working stronger every day to bring peace to the community,” Massillon said. “I’m optimistic that the state will continue working to eradicate the gangs in Kenscoff.” Gangs are coveting Kenscoff because it allows them to surround and control the upscale community of Pétion-Ville and alternate routes connecting Haiti’s capital to its southern region, said María Fernanda Arocha, a researcher with the nonprofit Armed Conflict Location & Event Data. Between January and August this year, security operations had managed to reduce violence in Kenscoff by 66% prior to the attack, she said in a statement. “While security forces have concentrated their efforts on operations aimed at regaining control in the central areas of Port-au-Prince, criminal groups have instead sought to expand into rural communities that are vulnerable due to the limited response capacity of the police, but which remain strategic hubs,” she added. Haitians demand police protection Some survivors accused the government of not providing enough protection prior to the attack, with Haiti’s National Police rejecting those accusations. Le Cour said that if police and armored vehicles were indeed stationed in Kenscoff prior to the attack, then the assertion is concerning: “You let the gangs come in even if you had everything in place?” Armed men control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince and swaths of land in Haiti’s central region and beyond. Gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti, where more than 3,050 people were reported killed from January to June and another 1,400 injured, according to U.N. statistics released Tuesday. The U.N. noted that nearly 800 rapes were reported from April to June, with 87% of those cases representing collective rapes. At least 81 people also were reported kidnapped during that time period, according to a new U.N. report. “These figures represent only a portion of the total number of people kidnapped,” it stated. “In many cases, victims’ relatives do not report kidnappings to the police or service providers and choose to negotiate directly with the kidnappers, believing that this approach allows for a quicker release and avoids possible reprisals.” The number of kidnappings reported from April to June represents a more than 40% increase compared with the previous quarter.

images.caption: People mourn over the bodies of people they said were their relatives and killed in a gang attack in the Kenscoff neighborhood of Port-au-Prince, Haiti, on Aug. 24, 2026.

articles.title: Hillary Clinton says Republicans ‘secretly cheering’ for Mark Carney amid US-Canada trade negotiation
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton claimed that Republicans are “secretly cheering” for Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney amid tension between Washington and Ottawa over trade. “I can’t imagine that even in the Republican cloakroom in the Senate, there’s much enthusiasm for going into a trade war with Canada,” Clinton said Monday night during an…
articles.body:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton claimed that Republicans are “secretly cheering” for Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney amid tension between Washington and Ottawa over trade.

“I can’t imagine that even in the Republican cloakroom in the Senate, there’s much enthusiasm for going into a trade war with Canada,” Clinton said Monday night during an event in New York.

She added that 40 percent of Ohio’s exports and 60 percent of Michigan’s exports go to Canada.

“I can’t imagine that the Republicans in those states, or literally anywhere in the country, are enthusiastic about this nonsense that [President] Trump is promoting, and probably secretly cheering Mark Carney for standing up to him and doing what he’s now doing on behalf of his country,” Clinton said.

Canada unveiled retaliatory tariffs Tuesday on the U.S. in the wake of President Trump’s fresh threats to heat up the trade war between the two countries.

Carney said Canada would match American tariffs “dollar for dollar” following 50 percent tariffs the Trump administration placed on more than $20 billion in Canadian goods that went into effect over the weekend. Ottawa’s retaliatory levies are set to go into effect Sept. 8.

The prime minister said Monday that Canada may have to use more precise retaliation to protect its workers and businesses as Trump threatens new 50 percent tariffs aimed at cars, trucks, auto parts and steel going into effect at the beginning of next year.

Throughout Trump’s second term, U.S.-Canada relations have been shakier than usual, with trade disputes erupting between the two countries and Trump talking about acquiring the U.S.’s northern neighbor as the 51st state.

When reached for comment, White House spokesperson Kush Desai said in an emailed statement that “if Hillary Clinton knew anything about Ohio or Michigan – or Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, for that matter – she wouldn’t have so humiliatingly lost to President Trump in 2016.”

articles.title: Second man charged with murder after house fire
articles.summary: Slawomir Alama is accused of one count of murder and eight of attempted murder.
articles.body:
A second man has been charged with murder following a fatal house fire in west London last week, the Metropolitan Police have said.

Emergency services were called to the property on Berkeley Avenue in Hounslow at about 01:15 BST on 19 August following reports of a fire. Nine people were taken to hospital.

Anna Kowalska, 50, died in hospital, and a 40-year-old woman remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. The remaining seven people - six men and one woman - have since been discharged after receiving treatment for minor injuries.

Slawomir Alama, 41, of Bath Road, Hounslow, has been charged with murder and eight counts of attempted murder.

He has also been charged with arson with intent to endanger life, possession of a class B drug, and possession of a knife in a public place.

Alama was arrested on Tuesday in Leeds, the Met said, supported by West Yorkshire Police.

He has been remanded into custody and is due to appear at Willesden Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

It follows the charging of Pawel Kulpa, 34, of no fixed address, who appeared on Monday accused of one count of murder, eight counts of attempted murder, and one count of arson with intent to endanger life.

Kulpa is next due to appear at the Old Bailey on Thursday.

articles.title: India police clash with protesters a month after Gen Z demonstrations
articles.summary: Police used water cannons and batons as a few thousand protesters broke through security barricades in Bihar’s capital.
articles.body:
Indian students and unemployed youth have clashed with police as they marched towards the residence of the chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, ruled by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s party, demanding access to jobs and transparency in recruitment exams.

The government forces in Bihar used water cannons and lathis – the Indian version of batons – as a few thousand protesters broke through security barricades in the state capital Patna, videos seen by Al Jazeera showed on Tuesday.

list 2 of 4 Will India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement force Modi’s BJP to rethink its politics?

list 3 of 4 India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement makes schools next battleground against Modi

list 4 of 4 India used pellets, grenades on Gen Z protests: What Amnesty report reveals

The demonstrations came a month after massive Gen Z protests in New Delhi pushed for the ouster of India’s education minister over alleged irregularities in conducting key competitive examinations.

The July 25 resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan also marked a significant political defeat for PM Modi, who has tried to maintain a strongman image , while India has continued to slide in multiple democratic indices under his rule since 2014.

Police in Bihar, home to about 130 million people, detained at least 25 protesters in Patna and released them later, according to the Indian Express newspaper.

Local police accused some protesters of attacking security personnel.

“Police will identify those involved in stone pelting at police and will take action against them,” Patna Police Superintendent Kartikeya K Sharma told reporters on Tuesday.

The protests began last week with unemployed youth demanding jobs, but they later expanded to include calls for education reform .

Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary said his office was “listening to every student’s voice”.

A delegation of student representatives met Bihar’s top bureaucrat, Pratyaya Amrit, after the protests. Amrit then told reporters that the discussion “was positive, and we were assured of a favourable response within a couple of days”.

The tight employment market in India makes government jobs, which offer long-term stability, a major draw for millions.

Since the massive youth-led protests organised by the online Cockroach Janta Party in New Delhi, there have been similar demonstrations in other states challenging both the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and opposition parties.

In southern Karnataka, members of a BJP-linked student body staged a protest near the state chief minister’s residence on Tuesday over alleged irregularities in recruitment for government jobs.

Bihar’s regional Education Minister Mithilesh Tiwari said the government had addressed students’ demands, without giving more details, and added that the door for dialogue remained “wide open”.

In New Delhi, the Cockroach movement has also announced a march next month to protest against what it says is the Modi government’s failure to fulfil several promises of change , including the withdrawal of police cases against protesters.

articles.title: India police clash with protesters a month after Gen Z demonstrations
articles.summary: Police used water cannons and batons as a few thousand protesters broke through security barricades in Bihar’s capital.
articles.body:
Indian students and unemployed youth have clashed with police as they marched towards the residence of the chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, ruled by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party, demanding access to jobs and transparency in recruitment exams.

The government forces in Bihar used water cannons and lathis – the Indian version of batons – as a few thousand protesters broke through security barricades in the state capital Patna, videos seen by Al Jazeera showed on Tuesday.

The demonstrations came a month after massive Gen Z protests in New Delhi pushed for the ouster of India's education minister over alleged irregularities in conducting key competitive examinations.

The July 25 resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan also marked a significant political defeat for PM Modi, who has tried to maintain a strongman image , while India has continued to slide in multiple democratic indices under his rule since 2014.

Police in Bihar, home to about 130 million people, detained at least 25 protesters in Patna and released them later, according to the Indian Express newspaper.

Local police accused some protesters of attacking security personnel.

"Police will identify those involved in stone pelting at police and will take action against them," Patna Police Superintendent Kartikeya K Sharma told reporters on Tuesday.

The protests began last week with unemployed youth demanding jobs, but they later expanded to include calls for education reform .

Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary said his office was "listening to every student's voice".

A delegation of student representatives met Bihar's top bureaucrat, Pratyaya Amrit, after the protests. Amrit then told reporters that the discussion "was positive, and we were assured of a favourable response within a couple of days".

The tight employment market in India makes government jobs, which offer long-term stability, a major draw for millions.

Since the massive youth-led protests organised by the online Cockroach Janta Party in New Delhi, there have been similar demonstrations in other states challenging both the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and opposition parties.

In southern Karnataka, members of a BJP-linked student body staged a protest near the state chief minister's residence on Tuesday over alleged irregularities in recruitment for government jobs.

Bihar's regional Education Minister Mithilesh Tiwari said the government had addressed students' demands, without giving more details, and added that the door for dialogue remained "wide open".

In New Delhi, the Cockroach movement has also announced a march next month to protest against what it says is the Modi government's failure to fulfil several promises of change , including the withdrawal of police cases against protesters.

articles.title: Two unvaccinated people die of measles in US state of Pennsylvania
articles.summary: Experts warn that declining vaccination rates have opened the door for resurgence of disease once largely eradicated.
articles.body:
The US state of Pennsylvania has reported that two residents died from measles , marking the first fatal cases this year of the disease that had previously been largely eradicated in the United States.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health said on Tuesday that both of the deceased were unvaccinated residents of Lancaster County, but did not share additional details due to privacy concerns.

“Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness,” said Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Debra Bogen.

The US is facing the most severe measles outbreak in years as vaccination rates drop below levels that medical experts say are necessary to confer herd immunity. That decrease has been partly driven by an anti-vaccination movement that includes prominent members of the Trump administration , such as Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr .

At least 2,777 confirmed cases of measles have been recorded in the US thus far this year. Pennsylvania has been among the hardest hit by the outbreak, recording 393 measles cases across 28 different counties.

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order earlier this month calling for the number of recommended vaccines for children to be reduced, continuing a push to roll back decades of scientific consensus on the safety and efficacy of vaccinations .

Trump and Kennedy, also known as RFK Jr, have pushed debunked claims linking vaccinations with autism and purged government health panels tasked with making recommendations on vaccine policy.

“We all thought the Texas outbreak and the deaths there last year would be a wake-up call. Then we had the outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah,” Dr Angela Dunn, former Utah state epidemiologist and previously a division director in infectious disease response at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, told the Reuters news service.

Three people died from a measles outbreak in 2025 that began in West Texas and spread to New Mexico.
